In the UK, BYDs are typically co-located with Peugeot or Vauxhall dealerships and he was coming from the Peugeot dealership next door.  His main comment was that the biggest hurdle with the BYD cars is the fact it's a Chinese car and there are a lot of people who just cannot get over the idea that it's a cheap knock-off of a Tesla.  The result is that they get far less visitors than the Peugeot but sales are higher because the conversion rate is much higher.  Once people get into the showroom they've already moved past that "Chinese Car Stigma" and the car just sells itself. 

I got a pre-reg car registered in November. It was £10k lower than list price and is costing me less than £400 a month including maintenance.

text:
Wow!   Don't really know how I landed on this video, but as a person who has received specialist training and loves to drive anywhere and everywhere (can't remember when I last took a bus or train!), I decided to watch your review all the way through.  I actually never knew that BYD was  car maker!!

Ok, my thoughts . . . as a Mercedes C Class petrol C180 Elegance driver (it's 20 years old, Petrol with 185,000 on the clock, but it goes so well), I have always said no to electric cars.   Why?  Ok I would want one that fulfils certain conditions that not one EV comes close to - yet.;   At least a 420 mile range with a 15 mile reliable reserve (note that ALL manufacturers overstate their vehicle ranges !!).   Milage - yeah, 323 miles, I don't think so.   I wonder what the driving conditions and speeds were for you to get 200 miles out of it? A decent cockpit too!   Having just returned from a holiday in the US, my rental car was like driving the bloody Space Shuttle!   Why can't manufacturers just do a good, simple instrument panel?   It took me ages to figure out how to start the car, select the lights, wipers and Air Con - and I never worked out the cruise control!   All this on a normal petrol car, just so much easier on the Merc!   

And I am dead against having a bloody laptop in the front driving area!!    Yes, all those fancy things are all well and good, but IMHO dangerous!   There was a time when having a "screen" in front was illegal!   If they are going to encourage people to switch to EV's then this sort of vehicle could really confuse the older generation who can still drive well and safely.   Lane assist?   Terrible idea!   I want to have a car that "I" drive, not have it drive for me.   As a specialist trained driver, I want to be in full control.   I had this on the US Rental car and it was a nightmare on the freeways!  I am happy to have things that are useful to me.   One really great utility on the rental car, was that it had small lights in the wing mirrors that alerted you when a car was really close (they pass on both sides on the freeways in the US!)  

Ok, don't get me wrong.   If I could find a car that meets all my wants then I would happily switch!   Maybe this car is a candidate?   But I would want to make sure that certain "assists" could be disabled before I took delivery.   I am very glad you are happy with this car.   The driving seat position also looks really good.   But I'm not sure I would be tempted to buy this yet.   I am waiting for seriously big improvements in range, battery life and overall usefulness, since in these cars, the battery powers everything;  Lights, Music, Air Con and all things electric - and it also has to power the drive train.   My Merc has a battery for all these electrical things and petrol drives the engine, so the engine can still run if the battery suddenly dies.

And £45700 for this?  Well surprise, surprise for an EV, I was quite astonished as it's a really competitive price for this vehicle!   EV's over 50 grand are not as feature rich as this car appears to be.   Oh, one other matter.   Keyless entry?  No thanks!   Real security risk!   Thieves now have the ability to electronically get into a keyless car and steal it away in under 15 seconds.   Coming from 38 years in the Security industry, I know how bad this is getting to be.

So, you got my attention and thanks for the review.   Very glad you possibly found the car you really want?   Let's hope they give you a good deal.   I will get rid of the Merc one day and I will look more closely at BYD.   All the best to you.   Lee (virtualairlinepilot.org)

Don't really know how I landed on this video, but as a person who has received specialist training and loves to drive anywhere and everywhere (can't remember when I last took a bus or train!), I decided to watch your review all the way through. I actually never knew that BYD was car maker!! Ok, my thoughts . . . as a Mercedes C Class petrol C180 Elegance driver (it's 20 years old, Petrol with 185,000 on the clock, but it goes so well), I have always said no to electric cars. Why? Ok I would want one that fulfils certain conditions that not one EV comes close to - yet.; At least a 420 mile range with a 15 mile reliable reserve (note that ALL manufacturers overstate their vehicle ranges !!). Milage - yeah, 323 miles, I don't think so. I wonder what the driving conditions and speeds were for you to get 200 miles out of it? A decent cockpit too! Having just returned from a holiday in the US, my rental car was like driving the bloody Space Shuttle! Why can't manufacturers just do a good, simple instrument panel? It took me ages to figure out how to start the car, select the lights, wipers and Air Con - and I never worked out the cruise control! All this on a normal petrol car, just so much easier on the Merc! And I am dead against having a bloody laptop in the front driving area!! Yes, all those fancy things are all well and good, but IMHO dangerous! There was a time when having a "screen" in front was illegal! If they are going to encourage people to switch to EV's then this sort of vehicle could really confuse the older generation who can still drive well and safely. Lane assist? Terrible idea! I want to have a car that "I" drive, not have it drive for me. As a specialist trained driver, I want to be in full control. I had this on the US Rental car and it was a nightmare on the freeways! I am happy to have things that are useful to me. One really great utility on the rental car, was that it had small lights in the wing mirrors that alerted you when a car was really close (they pass on both sides on the freeways in the US!) Ok, don't get me wrong. If I could find a car that meets all my wants then I would happily switch! Maybe this car is a candidate? But I would want to make sure that certain "assists" could be disabled before I took delivery. I am very glad you are happy with this car. The driving seat position also looks really good. But I'm not sure I would be tempted to buy this yet. I am waiting for seriously big improvements in range, battery life and overall usefulness, since in these cars, the battery powers everything; Lights, Music, Air Con and all things electric - and it also has to power the drive train. My Merc has a battery for all these electrical things and petrol drives the engine, so the engine can still run if the battery suddenly dies. And £45700 for this? Well surprise, surprise for an EV, I was quite astonished as it's a really competitive price for this vehicle! EV's over 50 grand are not as feature rich as this car appears to be. Oh, one other matter. Keyless entry? No thanks! Real security risk! Thieves now have the ability to electronically get into a keyless car and steal it away in under 15 seconds. Coming from 38 years in the Security industry, I know how bad this is getting to be. So, you got my attention and thanks for the review. Very glad you possibly found the car you really want? Let's hope they give you a good deal. I will get rid of the Merc one day and I will look more closely at BYD. All the best to you. Lee (virtualairlinepilot.org)

text:
I changed from a Tesla M3 LR to a BYD Seal Excellence 5k miles ago & few observations:

Negatives:
I've never seen the claimed 0-60 in 3.8s, it is always, always, always 4.2s regardless of soc or weather conditions. 0.4s is quite a big difference from the claimed performance which is disappointing.
The accelerator pedal feels muted, even in Sport. You mash the pedal & it feels like an internal combustion engine rising in revs & torque. The Tesla (& Polestar) I've previously owned had instant response to pedal inputs, ultimately that's not really an issue but the real issue is when you lift off the accelerator pedal, it doesn't stop accelerating at the same time as you lift your foot, it will continue to accelerate for a fraction of a second longer than you want. That fraction of a second feels longer when you're expecting the car to slow as soon as you lift your foot.
The front parking sensors are a waste of time. They only actually work if you drive forwards towards the object then select reverse to activate the front sensors. I've reported this to BYD & apparently this is a feature which is working as intended - total waste of time! Every car I've had for the last 15 years at least had front parking sensors that activated automatically when driving forwards slowly.
The latest UI update is much better except now on the main screen there is so much wasted space that could be filled with widgets / tiles
A/C in the summer isnt as cold as any other car I've owned since I can remember
On average for mixed m/way (70mph) & city driving I struggle to get 3miles/kW - the Tesla returned 4.2m/kW & was regulary drove at 80+mph on m/ways (I cant drive at that speed now because my range in the BYD falls off a cliff!
The drivers seat is not very comfy - under leg support needs increasing & the seat length needs increasing slightly to provide support to the lower part of my thighs (I'm only 5' 8")
The volume of the stereo is woefully low - I can have a conversation with my passenger whilst talking loudly (not shouting) when the volume is at 39 (max). For a claimed 750W system it is appalling, I cant understand why Dynaudio would allow their name to be associated with a poorly performing product
Rear view camera is pointless when driving in the wet, it is positioned to collect all the spray & crap off the road perfectly

Positives:
Build quality & materials are much better than most vehicles especially considering the price of the Seal
The interior of the Seal is a very nice place to be (with exception of the drivers seat on longer journeys) - very very quiet even at m/way speeds
The driver aids are not very intrusive & are easily turned off (speed limit warning) if you prefer. The Lane Departure Warning is probably the best designed on the Seal, it is probably the best version I have experienced in any other car
It looks pretty (in my opinion)
It has a relaxed but responsive chassis (not as hard / twitchy as the Tesla), it reminds me a lot of my old Volvo S90 for ride quality (that is a compliment)

text: Or you can have "bad luck" like the colleague in Finland and need to replace all the brakes at the 30,000-mile service. The BYD Seal is far from an okay car. It performs quite poorly in winter since it takes forever to warm up, leaks cold air into the cabin, and you can't defrost the windows from the mobile app, so you end up sitting in a cold car to heat the windows. The battery is cooled with AC gas, which is basically worthless but the cheapest solution. The UI is horrible, and after 1.5 years with several updates, it's no better. text:
I have owned the perfoirmance for roughly 2 months, aside from the battery/distance milage (I came from a standard ICE car with nearly 800km range), its an amazingly good car.
The performance has insane levels of torque, great to leaving people at traffic lights in the dust (without even breaking speed limits). I typically run the car in ECO but the sports mode is next level sports car enthusiast.
The interior is great. Highly reccomend the full leather. The boot space is great. The new sunroof has an electric shade so you dont have to worry about heat.
I heard a lot of people complain about the sound system but it just required a few tweaks and I still cant play it at full volume without hurting my ears. 
Recharge on 7kw single phase takes about 8 hours from 30% to 100% (assuming you run it down like I do and thats almost a week of to and from work). From 30% to 100% on 75kw at the local DC charging station is about 30min. This would be substantially less if there was a local DC charger that could do 150kw but I live in a more regional area and not in the city. I guess eventually the infrastructure will catch up. I just use the time to go shopping and come back to a full car.
Prices? Well I went from a petrol  v6 that was costing me around $100-$120 a week. Now I'm pulling around $30 a week on the public charger (which would be less half that if I had a  7kw charge port installed at house). The price goes up to about $45 at a DC charger (higher fees per kW). Needless to say that for a car that weighs over 500kg more than the previous petrol sedan, I'm very impressed.
Oh I live in Australia too.

text:
Looks are subjective, Tesla is more streamlined, BYD takes a more additional approach in my opinion. Front looks better than TM3 Highland, the back worse than Highland (BYD looks far too asian for my taste). Tesla gives a spaceship vibe, BYD standard car vibe, nothing good nothing bad.

Software design, UI structure, translations, animations, service mode, games, native built-in apps, mobile app integration, driver profile synchronization and portability between cars, as well as screen computer performance are 500 times better in the Tesla obviously, same as with Autopilot, BYD Seal autopilot can't keep it in lane centered on European roads in recent testing, Tesla does it no problem. BYD on the other hand offers Android Auto integration for example, while Tesla uses completely own OS.

Interior BYD has traditional design, Tesla again most things on the touchscreen. BYD offers premium upgrade to get a Heads up display, Tesla does not. Personally, having driven the Highland, I did not miss any display in front of me, but that is subjective and everyone definitely should test drive both!

Personally I don't like the glossy surfaces in the BYD interior, but this is personal taste.

Storage space is more in the Tesla, and frunk is bigger in the Highland. In the Model 3, the rear seats folded down do present a much flatter surface than in the BYD, making camping in the Tesla vastly superior. (plus camp mode in Model 3 is very nice). 

Model 3 also comes with Matrix LED adaptive headlights at no additional cost in Europe, which is a HUGE plus, especially driving long windy roads or on the freeway at night, BYD does not offer any such feature.

According to a review by an actual EV mechanic, BYD uses a legacy approach for the ABS sensor design at the wheel axis, which means it will be broken 100% in less than 8 years requiring extensive repairs. Additionally, BYD is heavier and bulkier than Model 3, with tires being too small to support it when doing erratic maneuvers, when compared to Model 3 the ESP had to engage every single time on BYD to keep it on the road.
Maintainability is far easier on the Tesla, because on the BYD, a mechanic needs half an hour to only unscrew the underbody shield (70 to 80 small screws) to even be able to diagnose any problem if such occurs. Model 3 uses like 5 big screws, done.

Tesla service centers are far more present here in Europe, I don't even know where I could take the relatively new BYD for repairs.

BYD has average working auto wipers, Tesla still has a problem with the wiper speed in rain (got better but still needs work).

Sound system definitely superior and louder in the Model 3 having listened to both.

Model 3 is more efficient than the Seal no question, need to charge less electricity as a result and saving money.

Fast charging speed is faster in Model 3 than BYD Seal

What I noticed is BYD is faking pictures of their car on the website, in real life the gap between wheels and chassis is bigger than on the pictures, but many Chinese car brands are doing this practice to make it look slightly better on marketing images.
Tesla images seemed normal for me.

Cheers!

I just had a test drive of a Seal Premium and Dolphin top range today. Seal has very attractive exterior when I see it in person. Nicely designed interior feels like traditional car interior with all the buttons so those who like physical buttons will like it. However, the deal breaker for me was the flimsy infotainment system and the lag of one pedal driving.  Also the dash screen was not designed in intuitive way so even though it displayed a bunch of information, none of them is useful while driving. Their hardware looked pretty good, however, they need to work on the software way much more. With the price gap of $3k from Tesla Model 3, I would go and buy a tesla Model 3. Seal has a value for people who don’t want many features from a car but for me Tesla is way more advanced in terms of feature wise. 

My conclusion is, BYD’s hardware almost matches Tesla’s one but the software and the features are far less advanced at this stage. No netflix, no YouTube, no browser, no sentry mode, no pin to drive, no pin to glove box, no auto hold on a steep road, having to start and stop the car and etc. are what it’s missing compared to. Tesla. 

Dolphine was quite good but the price range of over $45k AUD is not really attractive for what the car is.

Beware when the 12v LFP auxiliary battery dies the car can’t be jump started. There is no replacement at all in Australia. Wait time is over 2 months for a vital component. BYD uses a proprietary 12v LFP that is not standard like all the other manufacturers that uses a simple lead acid battery that can be replacement in less than 15 minutes. So if the car can’t jump start you can’t disable the electronic parking brake to be towed. The motors of the EPB needs to be physically taken off for the car to be towed. BYD sells thousands of cars and yet they don’t keep any vital spare parts. Also, it’s only warranted for 12 months even though it was meant to be more durable and last the life of the car. I’m just letting people know about this. I believe the BYD sea lion 6 and dolphin has the same battery. So good luck if it breaks down

text: I’m not buying the line that the styling could be from any maker. It’s fussy and typically Chinese. Compare this with Tesla 3 or Polestar 2 and the styling fussiness is obvious. You’d do well to watch experienced EV testers in Norway (like Kris Rifa ) who review vastly wider ranges of EVs over many years and have come to pretty clear landings on the Chinese offering. Not the silly excitability about how fast it accelerates of this review but hard nosed reality that these Chinese EVs really don’t have the depth of engineering sophistication and tech development beyond sheer speed that makes for a decent car. Bells and whistles (including those that clearly don’t work as intended) are not enough. BTW, how many of us really need or even get to use that performance? The test of value and quality is different to a silly boy racer thrill. They have a long way to go and we should encourage the Chinese to keep working at it. But let’s not offer false praise.

It's LFP versus "ternary lithium" where the "ternary" of a ternary lithium battery refers to a polymer containing three metal elements (= nickel,  cobalt, manganese or aluminum) which is used as the positive electrode. 
Meanwhile LFP batteries use lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) as the cathode material, where the "PO" bond is very stable and difficult to decompose.  LFP batteries are not prone to structural collapse or heat generation nor form strong oxidizing substances at high temperatures or upon overcharge or damage, thus providing enhanced safety over ternary lithium batteries.

text:
The most comprehensive and best review of the Seal I have seen yet.
Haven’t driven one, but have sat in and played with the infotainment, etc. The interior seems more premium than my Model 3. The seats are just as comfortable, it has better ventilation/hvac, a driver’s display and hud, Apple CarPlay/Android Auto, indicator stalk, real leather seats (ventilated as well as heated) and just a few more physical buttons. The displays are lower resolution than the Tesla and the likes of BMW and Mercedes and are perhaps the only thing that reduces the premium feel of the interior.
The boot is probably the biggest compromise. My M3 boot is probably my second biggest ‘pinch point’ (the first being no driver’s display). The Seal boot is smaller still. There is less storage considering boot (including underfloor) and “frunk”. I believe BYD missed a trick by slavishly copying (ahem, I mean taking inspiration from) the Model 3 and not making this a liftback. Still, if practicality is the main goal, then the Seal U will be better, in the same way that the Model Y is more practical than the 3.
Here in NZ, I believe the version of the Seal that will sell the best is the big battery, single motor “premium”. Apart from the extra motor and dampers (hence better performance) that the “Performance” Seal has, the Premium only misses out on a heated steering wheel and electronic child locks, but gains 50km of WLTP range.
According to the BYD salesman, the active safety features can be changed to “nag only” (my terminology) rather than mechanical intervention. Whether that is something that has to be set every time is yet to be determined. Certainly here in NZ, BYD seem more receptive to making tweaks after customer feedback than other manufacturers.
Just too much is absent or has been removed from the new Model 3 for me to consider it as an upgrade (driver’s display, blind spot monitoring, USS, radar, passenger lumbar support, indicator and gear selector stalks. So the Seal now becomes the front runner.

text: BEFORE you decide - try BOTH the BYD Seal in an AWD version as well as a Tesla 3 Long Range Highland. I did so (Europe) last week. Even if the Seal comes with a lot of quality it still feels like a version 1 car and I will definitely recommend to wait for a version 2, for the following 4 reasons: 1) In the Tesla you get a much more firm and direct driving experience. You feel it especially while steering and while accelerating. 2) Car efficiency measured as kW to milage is lower in the Seal, probably because of the higher weight (´+ 300 kilo) and poor brake regen. 3) In the Seal the Software UI  as well as the functionality feel like a generation or two older. Old school menues, different menues to control driving set-up, lot of scrolling up and down etc. Besides that parts of the SW didn't really work while I tested the car a week ago - especially the parts where assisted driving is involved. 4) DC charging is quite slower in the Seal (150 kW) than the Tesla (250 kW) which will leave you wating a lot at the charging stations. An overall conclusion is that the BYD Seal feels a bit like old school car compared to the Tesla.

text: Thanks for the review Paul. I test drove the Model 3 Highland, Seal Performance and Polestar 2, back to back today. I was hugely disappointed by the Polestar 2, far inferior and ridiculously expensive for what you get. I had seen so many glowing reviews on the Polestar 2 but my own personal assessment is that it is way overrated. I have a current model 3 and I didn't think the Highland was much different, other than better suspension (which is compromised by very soft tyres anyway) - and of course missing stalks. The winner was the Seal for my purposes and will pick up tomorrow. Much quieter than the other two cars. Despite reviewers claiming that the Highland is much quieter then the old model 3, I don't think it is (at least compared to made in china Model 3s). The only downsides to the Seal is the poorly calibrated lane keeping assistance, but I am hoping they will eventually improve this with a software update. I also prefer the one pedal driving in the Tesla, but again maybe they will add it to the Seal via a software update. That said, the Polestar has one pedal driving, but it was horrible in comparison to the smoothness of the Tesla, you are better off with it disabled in the Polestar anyway. The Tesla is also best in class for efficiency.  But you have to keep all this in perspective, because the Seal will always be much cheaper to "refuel" compared to similar performing petrol cars.

text:
Thank you very much for your interest in this topic. I also bought cars with animal skin leather seats before I did my research and got to know the industry. The most important thing is: With today's modern materials, you have nothing to lose, just to gain. You achieve the same kind of luxury and comfort or even better while having the same or better durability with less impact on humans, animals and the environment.

You can use fabric/cloth, microfibre or leatherette. The classic approach is using oil/plastic as source material. Overall, a vehicle contains about 300 kg plastic. A car seat needs about 5 kg plastic. So the overall plastic share for the seats is very low and it is at this moment the most efficient way to produce a car seat. A couple of litres of fuel equals a car seat basically. So if you want to save oil/plastic, rather look at consumption for energy, fuel and heating and to other car parts than the seat. Note that animal skin leather also always contains a plastic coating for durability. However, long-term we should of course find raw oil alternatives. So going further, seats can be made from recyclables (e.g. from PET-bottles or old fishing nets) or even increased share of plant-based materials (like pine oil, canola oil or start-up materials like Pinatex from pineapple leaves or Desertex from cactus fibre or the mixed-plant-based Mirum, so be seen at https://youtu.be/S1aNZeoatmE?t=525). On a calculation base, by ditching animal skin leather from car interiors, the amount of emissions (CO2e) is reduced by 85 (!) % (https://www.press.bmwgroup.com/africa-dom-easteurope/article/detail/T0403389EN/on-the-market-from-2023:-bmw-and-mini-models-with-vegan-interiors?language=en) - and that is a very conservative calculation. So it is at this moment the most important thing you can do to make car interiors more sustainable.

A good example for high-end luxury with ventilated animal free seats is the BMW X7 with Sensafin: https://youtu.be/1pRNkW9nrrw
And the Kia EV9 with plant-based oil share: https://youtu.be/6vXePQi_MAk
New leatherette materials can be superior in every aspect, even for cleaning: https://youtu.be/u94YXJ72UTA
More and more natural materials are rising: https://youtu.be/nRSsXEnwHDo

Also check out what the animal skin leather industry tried to with our channel: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nP_CvLlaFlI
For seeing how the animals are being treated and transported in the global leather industry, watch this footage: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tkjCAmq1_8E
Note that the footage is genuine and was recorded by a highly decorated investigative journalist in Germany I know myself personally.
Also a group of researchers and German journalists from public media could recent directly trace the connection between car animal leather production and illegal burning down Amazon rain forest: 
https://www.daserste.de/information/reportage-dokumentation/ard-story/videos/illegales-leder-video-100.html

In a high animal skin grade, the animals are specifically raised for this matter. However even if meat is the "first" misuse case, the hide remains a profitable body part. That means: If manufacturers put animal leather in a car and you demand it as a customer, you give your money to an industry that earns money by oppressing humans, animals and harms the environment, you make them more profitable. Alternatively, you could support industries with your wallet which try to improve the sustainability of materials. Also, if you turn the argument around to "meat is the waste of the leather industry" you realize that it doesn't make sense (and is ethically doubtful) to discuss the primary use of individual body parts of mammals. Mind experiment: You are getting slain down on the street; would it matter to you if it was for your smartphone or for your purse? Remember that animal skin leather is no different to fur, fur is just leather where the hair is still on. And fur is widely not accepted for clothing anymore, and of course not for cars.

We cannot change what we have bought in the past, but with more information and compassion we can change how we decide in the future.

For a great insight into sustainability in the automotive industry, you can also check out our extensive documentary:
https://youtu.be/-8gNXlRGngA

text:
Hello Thomas
My impression is that you get a lot less of a car for the money you spend on it. Everyone in the car industry was bragging about that the cheap Chinese cars will be more affordable... seems that there are a lot of naive guys out there to believe that. 
It's more expensive than a Tesla and it gets you less range, although you have an 82.5 kWh net capacity. To put that into perspective, the RWD Model 3 achieves 515 km WLTP with 30% less battery (LFP also), while the Seal RWD has 570 km. Then, the AWD Model 3 gets 600+ WLTP from a 75 kWh battery while the Seal gets Seal clubbed at 520 km. 
And it's not aerodynamics. Seal has a 0.219 cd value, so the extra weight and the inefficient motors makes me not bothering to consider it in the future.

Then there is the interior. Some parts feel cheap compared to something that you see on Hyundai / Kia cars, but they feel better compared to Tesla Model 3, However not as the price tag would let you believe.
The screens look best when they're turned off. Because when you turn them on, they look like the Head Units that you can buy from AliBaba or AliExpress. I was very disappointed to see that the layouts reminded me of some very cheap Chinese Head Unit that I installed on my old Honda Civic in order to get AA.
But the most obvious things were the knock-offs from other car manufacturers, that this car has: 
- the Tesla door handles
- the Bentley steering wheel
- the Leaf-like center-console with
- the Volvo gear selector and
- the 15" screen that simply has a lot of wasted space

The charging speed it nothing to write home about either. For some reason it started so slow for the first 2 minutes (under 10 kW). I thought that the charger was the culprit, but no... 
The battery charges itself in 48 minutes from 10 to 80%. To put that into perspective, my 2019 Kona 64 kWh charges in ~40 minutes in the same conditions, while having 77 kW peak power. Maybe not a very good comparison, when you look at the capacity, but with more emphasis on the time component. And my Kona has almost 5 years old tech in it.
And while it's rated at "150 kW peak", it never got more than 125 kW. The charger (300 kW EnBW) was providing 125 kW, the car showed 119 kW.

When driving, the humming at < 30 km/h was painful. I didn't got the chance to look into how can I disable it, but it was very annoying, particularly when you'd stop at a traffic light. In Hyundai / Kia, that sound is almost muted when the car comes to a halt.
Suspension was, indeed better than in Model 3, but again, you're expecting more for the extra money that you pay for it.
The car's prices are at least 3,000 € over Model 3, and you have pay an extra "surprise fee" of 1,300€ on top of that price. They call it "transfer fee".

text:
Thank you very much for your interest in this topic. I also bought cars with animal skin leather seats before I did my research and got to know the industry. The most important thing is: With today's modern materials, you have nothing to lose, just to gain. You achieve the same kind of luxury and comfort or even better while having the same or better durability with less impact on humans, animals and the environment.

You can use fabric/cloth, microfibre or leatherette. The classic approach is using oil/plastic as source material. Overall, a vehicle contains about 300 kg plastic. A car seat needs about 5 kg plastic. So the overall plastic share for the seats is very low and it is at this moment the most efficient way to produce a car seat. A couple of litres of fuel equals a car seat basically. So if you want to save oil/plastic, rather look at consumption for energy, fuel and heating and to other car parts than the seat. Note that animal skin leather also always contains a plastic coating for durability. However, long-term we should of course find raw oil alternatives. So going further, seats can be made from recyclables (e.g. from PET-bottles or old fishing nets) or even increased share of plant-based materials (like pine oil, canola oil or start-up materials like Pinatex from pineapple leaves or Desertex from cactus fibre or the mixed-plant-based Mirum, so be seen at https://youtu.be/S1aNZeoatmE?t=525). On a calculation base, by ditching animal skin leather from car interiors, the amount of emissions (CO2e) is reduced by 85 (!) % (https://www.press.bmwgroup.com/africa-dom-easteurope/article/detail/T0403389EN/on-the-market-from-2023:-bmw-and-mini-models-with-vegan-interiors?language=en) - and that is a very conservative calculation. So it is at this moment the most important thing you can do to make car interiors more sustainable.

A good example for high-end luxury with ventilated animal free seats is the BMW X7 with Sensafin: https://youtu.be/1pRNkW9nrrw
And the Kia EV9 with plant-based oil share: https://youtu.be/6vXePQi_MAk
New leatherette materials can be superior in every aspect, even for cleaning: https://youtu.be/u94YXJ72UTA
More and more natural materials are rising: https://youtu.be/nRSsXEnwHDo

Also check out what the animal skin leather industry tried to with our channel: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nP_CvLlaFlI
For seeing how the animals are being treated and transported in the global leather industry, watch this footage: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tkjCAmq1_8E
Note that the footage is genuine and was recorded by a highly decorated investigative journalist in Germany I know myself personally.

In a high animal skin grade, the animals are specifically raised for this matter. However even if meat is the "first" misuse case, the hide remains a profitable body part. That means: If manufacturers put animal leather in a car and you demand it as a customer, you give your money to an industry that earns money by oppressing humans, animals and harms the environment, you make them more profitable. Alternatively, you could support industries with your wallet which try to improve the sustainability of materials. Also, if you turn the argument around to "meat is the waste of the leather industry" you realize that it doesn't make sense (and is ethically doubtful) to discuss the primary use of individual body parts of mammals. Mind experiment: You are getting slain down on the street; would it matter to you if it was for your smartphone or for your purse? 

We cannot change what we have bought in the past, but with more information and compassion we can change how we decide in the future.

text:
@lifeliver9000  I've driven 2 of them. One with a salesman present for a 30 minute test drive, and the next day without a salesman for 60minutes. 
This is a great top trumps car, I.e. on paper it has all the spec. In reality, it's a really poor package. The steering is absolutely terrible, too heavy in any mode, too artificially quick to mimic sportiness and just makes it irritating to drive, the ride quality is substandard, when driving it hard (the 530hp car) the throttle response isn't calibrated correctly, when you floor it there's a pause before the power arrives and a when you lift off whilst at full throttle it takes a moment longer than it should to react. The menu systems are laughably bad, 7 presses on the screen required to turn off the speed limit alert system, similar for lane keep. You can't turn on Cruise control without the lane keeping coming on automatically. The lane keeping beeps like no other car I've test driven (and I've tested many). Both cars in the dealership had faults, on one car the electric seat height adjustment had failed and on the other it was prompted error messages about a reversing system error. The seats are soft initially, but once sat it for a longer period they are too hard underneath, low quality. Doing simple things like turning on a seat heater requires trawling through sub menus. I could go on and on...   People will naively buy because they are really cheap for the spec provided, and they'll end up hating the overall package.

text:
Hyundai and Kia have unveiled a radical new EV drivetrain system

Hyundai and Kia have linked up to reveal a new universally adaptable drivetrain system called the ‘Uni Wheel’, which aims to change both personal and commercial mobility and deep-fry your mind. 

The new system integrates pre-existing drivetrain technology that has essentially been re-engineered to move the main drive system components to the vacant area within a car’s wheel hub. Want to understand how it works? Get your nerd hat on, it’s time for a science lesson.

In a traditional combustion-powered car, the power is sent from the engine through the transmission and then to the wheels 

using drive shafts and CV joints. In an EV, the electric motor and reduction gear substitute for the engine and the transmission, but the rest of the process remains the same. 

The Uni Wheel looks to change this final step by repositioning the reduction gear in an EV to inside the wheel hub and then fitting ‘compact’ individual motors closer to each wheel. This would not only reduce the size of the drive shafts but also the amount of overall floor space used. That means more cabin space for crisps and crumbs to claim as their residence.
OK, ready to get even geekier?

What then allows the Uni Wheel to work is a ‘planetary’ gear configuration, which consists of a centrally-located ‘sun’ gear, four ‘pinion’ gears on each side, and a ‘ring’ gear that sits on the outer edge, posing as the asteroid belt in this particular section of the Solar System.

The power generated by the motor is first sent to the sun gear, which is then relayed to the pinion gears to move the ring gear. The ring gear, which is connected to the actual wheels of the car, then springs into life and enables drive. Keen engineering fanatics will also note that this system could even move the torque vectoring game forward since each wheel basically has its own engine.
The South Korean power couple also says this will have a positive impact on ride comfort since the drivetrain works closely with the multi-axis suspension to ‘stabilise’ the vehicle with quicker bursts of power and torque over rougher surfaces. 

The technology will continue to be refined with a view to incorporating it into future products and has the potential to be applied to anything with wheels as small as four inches or as large as 25.

That means it can even be used on different types of mobility solution, ranging from bicycles to wheelchairs. We're left wondering if it could enable a new racing series for delivery robots. ‘Formula Robot’ certainly has a ring to it, no?

The BYD Seal is manufactured by BYD (Build Your Dreams), a company that started in 1995 and is known for making batteries, including those for iPads and cell phones.
The car features BYD's blade battery, which is structurally integrated into the vehicle's floor, providing enhanced safety demonstrated through crash tests.
The BYD Seal is described as having driving characteristics similar to the Tesla Model 3, with a comfortable and controlled feel, a heads-up display, and an interior that is considered high-end and luxurious.

text:
This is nowhere near the best one they make either, in fact I'd say it's the worst small EV sedan they currently make in China out of like 10+ new models that came out this year. BYD is like a budget brand in China, like a Skoda in Europe for example. It's a mediocre brand and that's why they allow it to sell in Europe. 

The really good Chinese cars won't make it to Europe because it won't be allowed, they'd ruin our industry, or the EU will slam such taxes on them it will be financially impossible to buy them. Look up  cars like the Nio ET5, Xpeng P7 (co-developed with Porsche), Geely Galaxy L6, IM LS6 (800hp for 40k dollars), IM L7 sedan, which had the chassis co-developed by the Williams F1 team. Or the Roewe F7,  Aion Hyper GT, QiYuan A07, MG7, BYD HAN, Avatr 12, etc.  I mean, these are just new sedans released in the last couple of months. ONLY SEDANS. Didn't mention any other type, and they're all some of the best looking sedans you'll ever see, and better looking than anything any western established manufacturer is doing right now. China is making so many new cars it's mindblowing. Their car industry is booming in a way that no car industry in the world has ever done. We won't buy Chinese cars because they're cheap, we'll WANT to buy them because they'll be desirable because of their design, quality, performance, etc. That's just the reality the west has not woken up to yet. We've been overtaken, and we're already so far behind we couldn't even catch up if we tried, let alone if we're not aware that we're behind and live in a delusion that China is still making cheap knock-off cars. They're not. They're leading the way in tech and in design. They make the US car industry in the 50's and 60's look static in comparison, and that was a time when it felt like a new car model came out every week.

text:
Joe had been distracted by the newspaper headline as he had drifted around the supermarket during the weekly shop. Over £17,000 for a Tesla replacement battery! It had made him think hard about the real economics of electric cars, ready to explain to Fred how electric cars conceal their costs and why they are inevitably more expensive than petrol or diesel cars. 

Fred: (Beckoning Joe over as he polishes his new car.) Hey Joe, let me tell you about my electric car. It’s so economical to own.

Joe: Is it really?

Fred: Oh yes! Much better than that petrol car of yours. How much is that to run?

Joe: I suppose a full tank is about £70 nowadays. And I do about 500 miles with that. That’s 14p per mile. 

Fred: My electric car’s much cheaper than that. I can charge it at home overnight with electricity at 16p per kilowatt hour. And since I can go four miles for each kWh, that’s only 4p a mile – tons better than your petrol car!

Joe: Gosh that’s really interesting. To be honest I need a new car. My Focus had to have a new petrol tank the other day. It was a pain to get one because they are so rarely needed. Cost me £100 on eBay – plus the labour – £300 altogether. (He pauses. Naughtily he asks.) Do you know how much a new battery costs for your Tesla?

Fred: I’m not sure I do actually. I guess it’s a bit more than that.

Joe: Go on – have a guess!

Fred: I’ve no idea. Do you know?

Joe: Yup. Near enough £18,000.

Fred: What?!

Joe: Exactly. But they won’t tell you that. It’s only when you have problems that you find out.

Fred: They are expensive but they do last the life of the car.

Joe: So do most petrol tanks. It’s only because my Focus is 20 years old. 

(Both stand quietly, obviously thinking.)

Joe: (Breaking the silence) Tell me Fred, how many miles do you expect your fancy Tesla will do over its life? 

Fred: I suppose it will be like any other car – probably around 120,000 miles before it gets scrapped. 

Joe: So, when you think about it, that Tesla of yours, with its £18,000 battery lasting 120,000 miles… that’s (doing quick mental arithmetic in his head) 15p per mile just for the use of the battery. 

Fred: I suppose you could put it like that…

Joe: (Interrupting)….plus the 4p per mile to charge it…

Fred: I suppose so..

Joe: 15p a mile for use of the battery and 4p a mile to fill it up – a total of 18p per mile. That’s more expensive than my petrol car at 14p per mile!

Fred: That does make it sound expensive.

Joe: And when you fill it up, when you’re not at home, how much does the charging cost then?

Fred: Mmm… It can be a bit more.

Joe: How much? Tell me!

Fred: Well, I did have to pay 80p a kWh the other day.

Joe: What! 80p a kilowatt hour? To take you four miles? That’s 20p a mile – on top of your 15p battery costs, that’s 35p a mile – more than twice what my petrol car costs.

Fred: I don’t often have to pay 80p. It’s more usually about 40p but I suppose that’s 10p for charging plus 15p for battery costs. Yes… 25p per mile when you think about it like that. A bit more than yours. 

Joe: A bit more! It’s nearly twice as much! (Joe pauses) Yours is a Model 3 isn’t it? The long range model?

Fred: Yup.

Joe: I looked it up. About £50,000, am I right? 

Fred: Yes it was about that.

Joe: When you think about it, that’s £32,000 for a normal car, plus £18,000 for the battery. That’s how it works. I know you don’t think of the £18,000 for the battery as running costs but that’s only because you’ve paid them up front, when you bought the car. 

Fred: Makes sense. 

Joe: And I’m thinking about a new Focus for £32,000 and at that price has the petrol tank included. 

Fred: Mmm…

Joe: And costs 14p per mile to run – not somewhere between 18p and 35p.

Fred: (Half turning away) But I am helping save the planet!

Joe: (Joe remains quiet. He thinks he might have been too blunt. He ponders on the half ton of battery that Fred’s car has to drag around, the mines where they extract the rare battery chemicals, the impending piles of batteries needing so-called recycling all to ‘save the planet’. Out of respect for Joe, he tries not to snort audibly.)

Naughtily he asks.) Do you know how much a new battery costs for your Tesla? Fred: I’m not sure I do actually. I guess it’s a bit more than that. Joe: Go on – have a guess! Fred: I’ve no idea. Do you know? Joe: Yup. Near enough £18,000. Fred: What?! Joe: Exactly. But they won’t tell you that. It’s only when you have problems that you find out. Fred: They are expensive but they do last the life of the car. Joe: So do most petrol tanks. It’s only because my Focus is 20 years old. (Both stand quietly, obviously thinking.) Joe: (Breaking the silence) Tell me Fred, how many miles do you expect your fancy Tesla will do over its life? Fred: I suppose it will be like any other car – probably around 120,000 miles before it gets scrapped. Joe: So, when you think about it, that Tesla of yours, with its £18,000 battery lasting 120,000 miles… that’s (doing quick mental arithmetic in his head) 15p per mile just for the use of the battery. Fred: I suppose you could put it like that… Joe: (Interrupting)….plus the 4p per mile to charge it… Fred: I suppose so.. Joe: 15p a mile for use of the battery and 4p a mile to fill it up – a total of 18p per mile. That’s more expensive than my petrol car at 14p per mile! Fred: That does make it sound expensive. Joe: And when you fill it up, when you’re not at home, how much does the charging cost then? Fred: Mmm… It can be a bit more. Joe: How much? Tell me! Fred: Well, I did have to pay 80p a kWh the other day. Joe: What! 80p a kilowatt hour? To take you four miles? That’s 20p a mile – on top of your 15p battery costs, that’s 35p a mile – more than twice what my petrol car costs. Fred: I don’t often have to pay 80p. It’s more usually about 40p but I suppose that’s 10p for charging plus 15p for battery costs. Yes… 25p per mile when you think about it like that. A bit more than yours. Joe: A bit more! It’s nearly twice as much! (Joe pauses) Yours is a Model 3 isn’t it? The long range model? Fred: Yup. Joe: I looked it up. About £50,000, am I right? Fred: Yes it was about that. Joe: When you think about it, that’s £32,000 for a normal car, plus £18,000 for the battery. That’s how it works. I know you don’t think of the £18,000 for the battery as running costs but that’s only because you’ve paid them up front, when you bought the car. Fred: Makes sense. Joe: And I’m thinking about a new Focus for £32,000 and at that price has the petrol tank included. Fred: Mmm… Joe: And costs 14p per mile to run – not somewhere between 18p and 35p. Fred: (Half turning away) But I am helping save the planet! Joe: (Joe remains quiet. He thinks he might have been too blunt. He ponders on the half ton of battery that Fred’s car has to drag around, the mines where they extract the rare battery chemicals, the impending piles of batteries needing so-called recycling all to ‘save the planet’. text: Heat pumps have certainly improved energy handling of EV's, but please don't say that "you won't notice any difference", because that's simply not true. Instead of a 4.5 kW PTC heater, a heat pump will consume 1.5 kW for the same amount of heating energy. At an average speed of 75 km/h this still amounts to 20 Wh/km that is not used for propulsion. So the summer consumption at this average speed of 140 Wh/km will increase to 160 Wh/km, almost 15% less range. And when parking your EV outside in -10 °C for 1 day, will require battery heating that will result in some 25% range decrease. So it is better for sure, but still very much noticable!

Well, I recently had the option to choose a new lease car. I currently drive a 2020 Tesla Model 3 and I also test drove the BYD Seal. Honestly, I went a bit crazy with all the buttons in the BYD — way too much going on for my taste.

But the real deal-breaker? It doesn’t have one-pedal driving like the Tesla, and that’s something I really love. So... back to Tesla for me!

The updated Model 3 is great — looks nice, drives smooth, and it’s almost €10K cheaper here in the Netherlands compared to the BYD Seal. I can’t wait to get mine at the end of this month!

That said, I have to admit the BYD’s interior was pretty nice, and the big glass roof was impressive — almost like the one in the Model Y. But the Model 3 still wins it for me with more trunk space and a frunk. I’m not even sure if the BYD Seal has a frunk, but I often need all the storage space I can get.

text: The proliferation of touchscreen infotainment and HVAC controls during the past fifteen years are the greatest failure of automotive safety after the explosion of oversized personal vehicles. Touch screens are extremely useful for simplifying menus, particularly if they are menus that are rarely used, as older cars normally required some arcane knowledge of that particular brand in order to navigate certain backend settings. Using them for basic or routine controls serves no purpose beyond saving the manufacturer a small amount of money in R&D. They CANNOT be used purely from muscle memory, you have to take your eyes off the road in order to use them. Any control that must be used during driving becomes objectively more dangerous if a touch screen is needed, as it forces you to not only look, but to look long enough to confirm you have pressed the right button and that it registered it. This is why dials are better, but hey, who gives a shit about crashes and deaths due to distracted driving, look at the pretty screen!

text:
Marques has genuine influence, so it doesn't make sense to have "influencers" in quotations. How do you know their level of awareness to the average lifestyle? It's a starter EV because it is among the cheaper EVs that exist. I could be uninformed, but I've never heard of an electric car that costs even near $1,000,000. I doubt relatively poor people could afford any Tesla, so no, the Model 3 is probably not for "poors". No-one claimed to be of royal status, but I'd argue Marques is at least royalty-adjacent. Again, nothing shown or mentioned in this video costs close to $1,000,000.

     You're misunderstanding the word "starter", in this case it means the Model 3 is a good entry point into EV ownership. The Tesla Model 3 is one of the most accessible EVs on the market. It's got great performance, solid range, and lots of tech and features c͟o͟m͟p͟a͟r͟e͟d͟ to any other EV in the same price range. Combined, this makes the Tesla Model 3 a great option for someone entering the EV category. This is what "starter" means in this context. You can get a Model 3 for around $35,000 from Tesla, which is agreeably not cheap. Relatively speaking, however, it is somewhat cheap. Can you think of another EV which offers the same things for the same price? No, you can't, because it doesn't exist.

     Calling it a "starter" car isn't a classist remark, as if people should be starting with a Model 3, then be moving to something more expensive; it's a relative term to compare it to other EVs in it's class.

text: Completely agree with this content. I switched from 2020 Model 3 SR+ => 2024 Model 3 LR few weeks ago and while the looks are noticeably different the overall driving experience is a complete 180. It went from a light, fast, nimble, simple, and innovative vehicle to => a luxurious and hefty, fast, nimble, and more innovative vehicle, and for pretty much the same price I got my SR+. The display, including theater, camera, and recorded vids, is ~5-10x faster. As for the acceleration headrush, it's nominally faster than the SR+ until you get on the freeway - when it's a good idea to be conscious of the speedometer because I'm usually going 5-10mph faster than intended. It's different, and I will miss how light and effortless the 2020 SR+ felt but the 2024 LR deft feels like a step up.

text:
Most people don’t appreciate all the features that come with even the cheapest Tesla, and how easy it is to upgrade. Because it is software based Tesla can add new features as needed.

I had a Genesis, which is a Hyundai Mercedes copy. It came with auto folding outside mirrors that tilt down when you reverse, adaptive cruise control, heated and cooled seats, easy entry, power seats and windows, and a premium sound system. It had Apple Car Play, but it was wired. Unfortunately the nav software was provided by a third party so to upgrade I had to research how to get it, pay $125, download to a flash drive, and then plug the flash drive into the dash.

Every Tesla has all those features and wireless charging, plus features like dog and sentry mode, auto blinker shutoff after lane change, blind spot camera views and now red alert, green light alert at stop lights, and literally thousands more. All provided by a software update in the middle of the night.

This update process has no peer in the auto industry. Nobody talks about it in EV car reviews though, it needs a lot more visibility.

text:
Yeah Teslas are different. The sparse interior is a big change. However after driving one for a while you learn to love all the room, flat floor so no drivetrain hump, and ultra convenience. I set all features to auto. Headlights turn on when needed, and brights automatically turn on and off when needed. A drivers profile has all settings like seat and steering wheel position, easy entry mode, mirrors, climate, wipers, and driving mode, and each driver has a profile.

From your phone app you can precondition your car before driving so it’s all warmed up and ready to go. The car unlocks as you approach and locks when you leave the car.

I can open the tailgate with my watch app.

All commands like setting temp and fan speed, picking a song to play on Spotify, or changing the volume of the music can be done with voice commands.

It’s all different, and much better.

text:
Color is great, hell, I'll even go amazing on this one. Form is great. I've never been a fan of Tesla interior, and removing stocks and regular car cockpit/functions is just absolutely horrible design (I voted against Volvo EX-30 for same reason). But I absolutely despise Musk, what he has chosen to represent, and extremely bad business practices, so I never "fell for it" (despite looking good with performance to match). Those biased opinions aside, my warnings and negatives comes mostly from Tesla owners who have had theirs for a while and their experience with it as a brand. 

Just as suspected, while making a good *looking* EV when the rest produced abominations early on (now fully addressed), they had no expertise as an auto maker. Meaning quality would suffer. And referring to other videos by experienced owners, quality have been a severe issue. And I'm not talking about "quality" on a brand new vehicle, but quality down the line after having used it for a few years. Brand new "quality" doesn't mean anything, anyone should be able to get this right.

So with those in mind, I wouldn't recommend Tesla at all, for anyone. If there was anything I'd look up before a purchase from any brand, it would be looking up manufacturers history wrt bad consumer practices. If they force you to buy a whole assembly worth $4000 (self steering unit, happens to be Hyundai in this case, but many car manufacturers are extremely customer hostile these days - maybe all of them?) when it's a $140 part in that assembly that is broken and can easily be replaced - that's when you should just put them on the no-go list.

text:
I had a very scary experience with the new model 3 last weekend. I got an extended test drive during the whole weekend, so I tested it vigorously. I found myself constantly looking down before pressing the turn signal buttons before exiting roundabouts, particularly the smaller ones. Otherwise, it's impossible to hit the correct button, and even then it's too easy to hit the wrong one. I found that I lost track of my surroundings and became way too distracted at times because of this. 
One time I almost hit a pedestrian when exiting a roundabout. I was too focused on finding the button to press. I only looked down for a few seconds, but that was enough. When I looked up, a pedestrian was suddenly right in front of me and I had to slam on the brakes. Other cars behind me had to do the same and nearly hit me from behind. That really scared me. I've been driving for 20 years, and I've never been close to running over anyone before. I think these buttons are dangerous and shouldn't be legal. it's the only thing keeping me from buying one. I loved so many of the upgrades, so this was a real shame. I really liked the car, but I'm not sure I would ever be comfortable using this.
I live in the EU by the way, and we have roundabouts everywhere. It's probably not much of an issue in the US though.

2:46 - How did they get away with NO visible lights on the body of the car while the trunk is open? 
Lights MUST ALWAYS be visible to oncoming traffic even while the trunk is open. This is a safety requirement by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) on ALL vehicles. e.g. If you are parked on the side of the road (especially at night) and your trunk is open because you are loading stuff, oncoming vehicles NEED to see you. They can't see you if the Tail Light is up in the air. This why manufactures always split the lights if the light is attached onto a moving part (trunk) of the vehicle. 
Tesla ignored this this. Expect a safety recall soon.

text:
Just had a test drive. First  Tesla I have ever driven, after testing many other EVs. 

I drive an ICE BMW, so never owned an EV.

This Tesla is by far the best EV I have tested. It simply blows the others away that I have tested, and that includes the BMW i4 and iX1, Audi Q4 e-tron, Polestar 2, Volvo XC40 Recharge, Nissan Ariya, Smart #1 and Toyota bz4x.

I tested the entry level single motor car. To be honest, it was more than quick enough for me, faster than my 265hp BMW.

The ride was superb on the potholed roads of Stockport in the UK. It was super quiet inside, with far less tyre roar compared to my BMW.

I also liked the accurate and responsive steering, it gave me total confidence over control and placement of the car in multilane lane traffic.

As for the lack of steering wheel stalks, that took maybe two minutes to get used to. While the steering wheel mounted controls for indicators and wipers are unconventional by traditional car standards, I quickly found them very intuitive.

So, as I expected, the Tesla Model 3 is clearly the best EV in my price range. It is simply next level compared to offerings from the “heritage” brands out there.

text:
Just drove a RWD one at Fremont. Coming from our 2018 RWD, it's definitely a big upgrade in most departments. We don't have the double-glazed glass or extra sound deadening that the 2020s got, nor do we have eco tires anymore, so it's hard for me to say how much of the improvement is from  2020 vs 2024 updates. But it's just INCREDIBLY solid and quiet. I was super impressed. I like the interior improvements and tweaks a lot, too. The new wheel, especially being heated, is awesome. I found it odd that MKB was so outspoken about the stereo, and it being a "mini Model S". The stereo on our 3 punches WAY above its weight for the era. My father has a 2017 S and the stereo is *awful*. I'm sure the S got a much better system over the years, but the 3 was way better than the S when it was released.

On the downside, the lack of stalks. Sorry, that's a deal-breaker for me. Even the stalks on our 3 (and on my X5) that don't stay where you put them, are bad. BMW came to their senses and went back to stateful stalks, but Tesla learned the wrong lesson. The swipe-to-drive is okay but awkward, again, a downgrade.
On the styling front, while I like the new headlights and the leading edge of the new bumper, the rest of the front bumper is a bland downgrade. The loss of the lower lamps and foglights and the scallops in front of the front wheels makes it look really plain. 


Rear lamps and signals are an improvement, at least they're still amber (had to retrofit 2020s on our car).

1) It's much smoother. This is the biggest improvement by far.

2) I do not like the steering wheel that much. Not just because of the missing stalks, but the overall feel just isn't as nice. They've also put the leather stitching on the back of the steering wheel instead of the inside, which means you can feel it with your hands whereas you couldn't before.

3) I did not find the sound system to be noticeably better. The mid-bass which I can feel in my chest in the 2022 Model 3 does not hit as hard in the 2024 version, even though the volume of the bass is still very high. I think this is because they're using the subwoofers for some of the frequencies which would have previously come from the door woofers, but I'm not sure.

4) I still prefer the exterior look of the old one. The front of the new one is a bit boring in my opinion.

text:
I know this comment is quite late, but having owned this car for more than a year, I can confidently say that I didn't even notice that the buttons aren't physical at first. They feel like you're actually pressing a button. The tactile feeling is well done, and it works 100% of the time. I actually ended up preferring it over stalks when I got used to it and realized that when driving my sister's Kia occasionally. Almost zero movement with my hand required, super easy to use. The only time where it's bad is if my wheel is upside down, and it takes an extra second to look down, which rarely happens and it's always at slow speeds anyways. 

That said, the car did run into a low-voltage electrical issue at around 16,000 miles. It was taken care of promptly and for free by tesla technicians, but I feel like it shouldn't have happened in the first place. Additionally, I could hear occasional faint rattles after around 20,000 miles for around 20% of my drives (yes, it only happens sometimes. Most drives are completely rattle-free). Not horrible, but annoying when it happens but easily masked with music. Finally, the actual range is only around 260 miles at 80% (quoted 360 miles at full, so around 35 miles less than expected. Not bad, but probably lower due to it learning from my driving habits). 

Overall, he car is honestly amazing and fantastic to drive every day. For its price point, I don't think it gets any better.

text:
For everyone looking forward for a refreshed Model 3 Performance. Possibly called “Model 3 Ludicrous”

Now we know Musk has said that he won’t do a Plaid Model 3 because it would “complicate” the Model 3.

I believe that what he means by this is that putting two Plaid motors in the rear would require so many design changes that it wouldn’t be worth it. However, that doesn’t mean a Model 3 couldn’t get extremely fast with just two motors.

Just look at the trap speeds of a refreshed Model S LR. They are hitting 130+ mph in the 1/4 mile but they really aren’t that much quicker in the 1/4 mile because their 60 foot times are even slower than a Model 3 Performance.

However, if you go back to older Model S Ludicrous cars you can see that those cars could hit sub 1.6 60’ times but they were only trapping about 4 mph more than my Model 3 Performance with weight reductions.

The key here is if you simply combined the top end pulling power of the current Model S LR with the launch modes of the older Model S cars and put it in a Model 3 you would get ridiculous times with almost no complexity added to the Model 3.

The Model 3 doesn’t need three motors to be fast. It doesn’t even need Plaid Carbon wrapped motors to be fast.

It just needs to be able to do a proper launch and be able to hold max power at higher speeds.

If we could turn a 1.60 60’ with a 128+ mph trap speed the Model 3 Ludicrous would probably be able to keep up with a the Corvette E-Ray(10.4) in the 1/4 mile.

I honestly think they might be able to do that with the current 82.1 KWh battery and the two Model S LR motors.

Some of the P90D cars could hit 2.8 second true 0-60 mph times without subtracting rollout. They were hitting plenty of power with less than 10% more battery power than the current Model 3 Performance has.

The current battery is capable of producing plenty of power. You just need motors that can take that power at much higher speeds.

If they do a Model 3 Ludicrous this year I actually think it will be quicker than people are expecting but it won’t have a vastly different batttery or even vastly different motors. I think 10.4 @ 128+ mph is possible and possibly even 0-60 mph in 2.5 seconds. 

As of right now, The absolute quickest acceleration in the Model 3 Performance is achieved when the battery pack temperature is between 125 to 137 degrees Fahrenheit, the State of Charge is 100%, and the motors are as cold as possible. That will give you a “Max Discharge Value” of 629 HP or 462 KW at the battery.

A Model 3 Performance would probably dyno at 538-545 WHP if it was new and fully optimized.

Let us know what kind of times you are expecting if they produce a Tesla Model 3 Ludicrous.

The car had already been attacked by rust after one winter. This is due to a total lack of rust protection, mixed materials and a far too thin layer of paint.

Now the Danish FDM, the equivalent of the Motormen in Sweden, has gone through the warranty regulations for the most common car brands, where, among other things, rust protection and warranty are one of the parameters.

In the report, which was presented in March 2023, FDM notes that Tesla's warranty is deficient in some respects.

On the one hand, it does not cover all the mechanics connected to the electric drive, which FDM considers to be a consumer requirement. The charging cable, the high current connector and the batteries do not have full warranty coverage.

However, it is the rust protection guarantee that is the worst.

It does not cover paint damage or rust damage, which does not come from the inside.

The warranty terms state: “The Limited Lifetime Body Repair Warranty covers repairs resulting from pitting and deterioration of body parts, but excludes damage caused by rust”.

Just rust through
We Car owners have also noted Tesla's flawed rust protection warranty, which only applies to rusting through, and asked rust protection specialist Thomas Widström about what rusting through means:

“It is extremely rare. It is basically completely impossible for a car owner to prove where the rust has come from," says Thomas Widström.

For those of you who are thinking of giving your Tesla your own good rust protection, however, also have to think twice. This is what it says in the rust protection guarantee:

"Corrosion and paint defects caused due to or as a result of accidents, paint treatment, abuse, negligence, improper maintenance or operation of the vehicle, installation of an accessory, exposure to chemical substances."
The warranty expires
If you treat the undercarriage of your Tesla yourself, it counts as "exposure to chemical substances" and the rust protection then ceases to apply.

This is where Tesla differs from the crowd.

Most other car brands accept that the car owner himself supplements with paint and anti-rust treatments. But in Tesla's case, the warranty then ceases to apply.

Norwegian rust company Funderud Antirust took apart a Model Y to examine the car. According to the film, the rust protection of the best-selling electric car has major flaws, despite a 12-year rust protection guarantee against rusting through. Among other things, exposed areas are not covered by inner screens, the chassis is not galvanized and there is no undercarriage treatment at all. The paintwork is also considerably thinner than on most other cars. Where steel and aluminum meet, galvanic corrosion can also occur.
- We see that there is no PVC wear coating in either the spring tower or the chassis. And we notice the sheet metal joints here. There is no seal in the joints of the plate, which means that salt and water can seep in between.

text:
Great review Marques. Thanks for just being yourself and not trying to be smart, funny or hyping it up. Nice change from many wannabe youtubers!
😀
I've recently ordered a 2024 built M3 LR AWD here in Australia. I've asked for a 2024 birthday vehicle, so hopefully not too long a wait. Our vehicles come from the Tesla China factory but are almost identical to the U.S. one. I also really like the new red, but it's a AUD$2600 premium, so I ordered the standard white which is the easiest colour to touch up those stone chips with a toothpick thrown our way by other road users.

I compared the M3 with the BYD Seal (not available in the U.S.) The Seal was cheaper and possibly slightly better value than the M3, but ground clearance was lower than the M3 so I had to cancel my order as I didn't want imminent damage to the underside of the front bumper on my steep entrance to my carport.
Looking forward to the M3 LR. I love one pedal driving knowing the disc pads will likely last the life of the vehicle. Even with all the roundabouts here in Australia I'll just have to get used to having no indicator stalk, which is the only real complaint I have - and no heads-up display which would have been a plus for most drivers.

It is nice that you are happy with the update.

The internal all-around LED lighting "...which you'll notice, especially as you are driving..." sounds like a drawback. I don't want a distraction in the car as I am driving at night.

Deletion of the stalks was definitely a bad move.

That dashboard fabric has got to go. Aftermarket wood will hopefully be available.

The rear display screen is pointless. I have zero interest in back seat passengers being entertained.

As you got low by the headlights, it has circles in the front bumper, so hopefully that isn't an emergency hood release and is Tesla keeping that spot available for ultrasonic sensors once it sinks in that deleting those was a mistake.

Anyway, for me, it seems like the best plan is to go with a 2022 or pre-Highland 2023. Then, after some of these refreshes get into accidents, buy the doors from a salvage yard to have the double-glazed windows. Thus, getting the one important improvement and not sacrificing any of the good things.

Just a shame Tesla cookie-cutter manufactures these. If we had a menu to select the things we like from the pre-Highland version and add what we like feom post-Highland and delete what we don't like from post-Highland,....then we would be truly custom ordering our car.

text:
I own a 2019 and 2023 Model 3. Recently, a kid hit my 2019 with his truck, so I have been able to enjoy a rental Audi A5 Sportback. 

I was very excited to drive a comparable German sports sedan. The Audi I think is around $55K, so more expensive. And the Audi is only 100lbs lighter. It's got a nice interior. 

But the Model 3 is a far, far sportier car. Compared to the Audi, the Tesla has got direct steering feel. Its handling is flat, neutral, and completely controllable. Throttle response is instant, and has enough power to deliver whatever you need to do. 

The Audi is awkward. You step on the gas pedal, and you wait a second as it feels like it's bogged down, then without warning, the turbo kicks in for angry acceleration, even if you don't want it. In the most "dynamic" setting, the car is numb, and it reminds me of my 1981 Buick Regal I had in high school. You'll never upset the chassis in the Audi because it's so underpowered. And, it's no fun to drive. 

To add insult: I can't figure out how to refuel the Audi from my house. I have to stop at gas stations. 

I can't wait to get my 2019 Model 3 back from the shop...

text:
oh no, blinkers as buttons is a v bad idea. There were where they were in most cars because it was practical to turn the steering wheel and on the way just nudge the stalk in a direction the wheel is turning with your finger. It was obvious and intuitive. With buttons you need to remember that right is up, left is down, and if the wheel is already turned 90 deg anticlockwise (on a roundabout for example), suddenly right blinker is the button on the left. How does that make any sense? Not to mention that you don't just turn the wheel holding your hands in the same spot, you kinda always default into holding the wheel more or less on the same level, in the middle. Meaning, at 90 deg, the buttons are at the bottom of the steering wheel, and you need to reach down to them (and figure out that the right blinker is on the left actually lol). I get that this wasn't a consideration in the US because you guys have like 10 roundabouts in total, but in EU and basically anywhere else they are everywhere, in different sizes, different angles of exit etc, so muscle memory won't help here, and IMO, even if it did, it still seems dangerous or inconvinient at best.

This is objectively, the worst design choice in a car I've seen in a while. And I don't understand why they did it to begin with. I see 0 benefits. If it was for minimalism, I can't see how a button in front of you is more minimalistic than a thing sticking out behind the wheel that you can't see for most of the time, because, well, its behind the wheel :D
Just innovation for the sake of innovation. The worst kind.

Thankfully in EU this won't be allowed (right?)

Also, where is the horn button? I don't see anything in the middle... is it in the menus or what happened? (that was btw already played around with in Renault cars from around 2010s. Everyone hated that they moved the horn from the middle, to a stalk in front of the blinkers. Why? Who knows, they are french, nobody understands them anyway).

---
PS. Great vid as always Marques!

This allows even kids to be superior thinkers from an engineering perspective. I'm not optimistic about this change occurring tho.

text:
Upgraded from 2020 Model 3 (which I loved to death and couldn't even imagine how it could ever be improved aside from body/trim issues) => 2024 Model 3 LR few days ago. Oh boy, the difference is like switching from Camry to BMW 3. The overall heft, the way doors open/close, overall trim, handling, mood lights, no-stalk driving, backseat screen, ventilated seats, improved struts, etc., all make it feel like a completely different class of car. Highly recommend.

The 1 and only negative is that it feels a bit heavier - what I liked the most about my 2020 Model 3 was that for a very heavy car it felt so light and handling overall felt so effortless like a work of art. 2024 Model 3 LR on the other hand feels a bit more like a hefty luxury car with, and it leads to more physical exertion when handling.

text:
Yeah!!! The embargo is lifted and we can see this car...Finally! I must add that you missed perhaps THE most exciting thing about this car = The new adaptive suspension. Usually there's a tradeoff dilemma for engineers - to make it daily/liveable, meaning too soft for sporty driving or race car harsh wherein potholes, heaves, asphalt patches, expansion joints and speedbumps jar your 
teeth. All the best cars from Germany any and even Cadillac ( MRC or Magnetic Ride Control ) offer adaptive damping that assesses road conditions, speed and turning force to provide accurate compliance for the situation at hand. This system is automatic or user configurable as well, so have at it as you please. Track mode v.3 is an upgrade too with new tweaks. The new wheels are lighter, too.

The suspension has new geometry and the brake pads , while not carbon ceramic, are new and improved over the last gen Performance 3. It would be nice, Elon, to have some new, differentiating colors other than the same six choices you've offered for the last 6 years as seen on millions of other Teslas. 

The seats look amazing yet I agree those steering wheel buttons need to have a tactile click. Its not a deal-breaker for me, but no stalks and no gear shifter are weird. I know there's Auto Drive like in the Plaid and people say it works well, so maybe that would make up for that omission...to me.

The Ioniq5N is a wagon and the looks don't do it for me. Its also slower and over $70,000.. The fake transmission and phoney engine noises are controversial. In my brain, when manufacturers create fake engine noises for EVs ( hello Porsche ) they lose me. Its like fake news - Intellectually, I know it's BS. Some OEMs cut the gears slightly different in their sporty EVs which creates a true, mechanical sound that is pleasing and communicates sensations of speedier motation.

All-in, I'm stoked to drive it and may trade in my 2018 Long Range. Next comes the price. If it's signicantly less than a Hyundai N or BMW, it'll be a no-brainer. Being the most American car you can buy also helps. A new S Plaid still tops $90,000 with wheels and paint. Maybe a used Plaid? Love the hatch but its a big car.....

Thank you for making this video and I hope you can give it a go on the track soon!

GM did an incredible job with the Hummer EV, and it bodes well for their next gen EV’s elsewhere in the company.

Either way, great car. I'm glad I bought a pristine 2023 Model 3 Performance for 40k. Saved a bit of money and I prefer its styling and its real stalks. I know I'll sweat in the summer if I wear shorts on those "vegan leather" seats! :D
