text:
And if that bothers you that much, you can likely get an 18 inch aftermarket wheel for it to regain some if not most of that range back.

But in my experience with my Model Y, long distance travel has gotten a lot easier overall in a Tesla because they keep adding more and more superchargers in many places, so going as far as you absolutely can on one charge is less of an issue than how fast can you charge at each station you do stop at.

Or as Out of Spec Motoring calls it, "supercharger hopping". While you do have to stop more often, your overall trip is usually faster because you're spending less time at said superchargers compared to doing long deep charges at fewer ones that the car tends to do if you don't want to optimize the trip speed.

At one stop, it told me to deep charge for about 40 minutes to make it to the next supercharger which was about two hours away. If I was eating at a restaurant, that might've been fine. But since it was the middle of the night, I instead picked the next supercharger in between where I was charging and where the car wanted me to go. I only had to charge another 5 minutes to make it to the next one, then stopped at that one for maybe 15 minutes, compared to if I did the 40 minutes it originally wanted me to do.

This doesn't always work of course, because if the supercharger is full or you're at a V1/V2 supercharger, you'll probably have to wait. Should also be interesting as more non-Tesla EVs are able to use the V3/V4 superchargers and how they'll impact Tesla owners.

Needless to say, he is massively underwater on his car loan. Teslas experienced abnormal depreciation rates due to a double whammy: Tesla repeatedly raised prices throughout 2021 and into 2022, meaning they had to reduce prices throughout 2023. Then, federal tax credit was reintroduced to 3/Y. IMO, Model 3 had no business starting at $47k *before* taxes and fees. The depreciation that we recently saw won’t be seen again for a long time. It sucks that cars from various brands experienced massive depreciation over the past 2 years or so, causing many people to be underwater on their loans. But that should teach people not to bite off more than they can chew. At the end of the day, cars are depreciating assets, not investments. Either buy with cash, or put down at least 35% before getting into a loan. A car losing its value ideally should not significantly impact your net worth.

Buying Tesla excitement turned into disappointment, fraustrating, anger and Nightmare from Tesla Stockton, CA and Rocklin CA.

Was full of scratches on truck glasses and dent. I was very disappointed but still let it slide hoping will get a better quality and reject it. There was another Model Y stock in Tesla Rocklin. CA. So they fixed my delivery day to May10th,2026. With the Mother’s Day and my mom’s birthday I told her gonna be bit late for that since I was scheduled to get the car. Two days prior, I sent message to Tesla Team from Stockton and Rocklin,CA.
These are my exact message
“Hello ,
Sorry to bother you. I am going to pick up vehicle on May 10th, Sunday.
My humble request since I don't want to be disappointed  picking up vehicle again. Can you please advise Rocklin, CA  Tesla to check scratches, and other quality issues for me before delivering the car. Not anyone's fault. I just want to  get the car and get out of there happy as a happy customer this time. 
Thank you
They replied to me

“Hello from Rocklin Delivery! Yes our detail team will make sure to inspect the vehicle inside and out. If there are any imperfections from the factory, we will make note of it and set an appointment for you to get them fixed! You will have a smooth delivery regardless!

We will make a note to charge the vehicle to 100%.

So went to Rocklin. CA to get the car on May 10th, 
The car was ready and I did the inprction. Frunk trim was not aligned, no back light reflector, chip on driver side door.door bit hard to close and advisor told me just because of the new rubber.shield.
Advisor told me if I stop by Stockton Tesla, they will put it for me
Didn’t have my car I decided to take it since advisor told me it will be fixed at the service. 
Very disappointed fraustrated. I had a promo code for 3 months of FSD. Stockton Tesla  promised me with me with another 3 months of FSD while on first visit and on second visit another promise 3 months FSD from  Rocklin, CA total 9 month but still not showing.
Came home tried to open the glove box it open just a bit and look at underneath is vented trim under the glove box. went to Stockton Tesla, They put in reflector for me and scheduled for May27th.
my car buying experience inn30 years, this is the worse. Sales people just ignore you. Worse then small local dealers. I have all the pictures of defective. If I ask them for manager to talk they simply text me back to schedule maintenance. 
I really regret buying Tesla

📺 "Driving Tesla's Cheapest Car | First Review of the 2026 Tesla Model 3 Standard"
by Edmunds Cars
📊 298,769 views | 1,841 likes | 285 comments  |  🏷️ review

⭐⭐⭐ EXECUTIVE SUMMARY ⭐⭐⭐
The 2026 Tesla Model 3 Standard is positioned as the cheapest car in Tesla's lineup, saving buyers over $5,000 compared to the Premium model. Despite a simpler suspension and a smaller battery, the vehicle retains its core driving dynamics, premium interior feel, and essential features like the panoramic glass roof. The reviewer concludes that the minimal compromises make the Standard model the default, logical choice for most buyers.

⭐⭐⭐ DETAILED BREAKDOWN ⭐⭐⭐
The video provides a comprehensive first drive review of the 2026 Tesla Model 3 Standard, the most affordable vehicle in Tesla's current lineup, priced around $38,630. Presenter Alistair Weaver questions whether this cheaper model suffers from aggressive cost-cutting, similar to what Edmunds observed in the Model Y Standard. 

Starting with the exterior and interior, the changes are minimal. The car features new aerodynamic wheel covers and subtle interior material swaps, like fabric replacing some vegan leather. Crucially, unlike the Model Y, the Model 3 Standard retains the panoramic glass roof and double-glazed front windows. While the rear infotainment screen has been removed—a change the presenter actually praises for family use—the cabin remains comfortable, well-appointed, and avoids feeling like a 'poverty spec' vehicle.

On the road, the Model 3 Standard features a less sophisticated suspension setup compared to the Premium model. However, because the sedan sits lower to the ground than an SUV, body roll is easily managed, resulting in a drive that still feels sporty, responsive, and traditionally Tesla. The smaller battery pack slightly reduces acceleration and range (claiming 321 miles), but the real-world performance remains punchy and more than adequate for daily driving.

Finally, the review touches on Tesla's autonomous driving software. A notable downgrade is that the standard Autopilot in this trim will no longer auto-steer on the highway unless the driver pays for the Full Self-Driving (FSD) upgrade—a move Weaver criticizes as a cynical marketing tactic. Despite this, the overall verdict is highly positive, declaring the Model 3 Standard as the smartest buy in the lineup and a formidable competitor against rivals like the Hyundai Ioniq 6 and Chevy Equinox EV.

⭐⭐⭐ KEY TAKEAWAYS ⭐⭐⭐
🎯 The Model 3 Standard retains premium features like the panoramic glass roof and front double-glazed windows, unlike the heavily de-contented Model Y Standard.
🎯 Despite a simpler suspension, the car's low center of gravity ensures it remains sporty, engaging, and limits body roll.
🎯 The rear infotainment screen has been removed and replaced with physical air vents and USB-C chargers.
🎯 Standard Autopilot on this model is software-limited and will not automatically steer on the highway unless the driver purchases the FSD upgrade.
🎯 At roughly $38,630, the minimal compromises make this trim the best value and default choice for most Model 3 buyers.

⭐⭐⭐ ACTIONABLE ADVICE ⭐⭐⭐
💡 Opt for the Model 3 Standard over the Premium version if you want to save $5,000 and do not require maximum range or track-level performance.
💡 Be aware that to get highway auto-steer functionality, you will need to pay an additional $99/month for the Full Self-Driving software.
💡 Use the frunk (front trunk) for versatile storage, as it remains fully functional and lined, unlike some downgraded models.

text:
The Autopilot helped me eliminate Tesla from possible EV's I'll consider buying. I have a VW Alltrack with Adaptive Cruise Control very similar to Tesla cruise control, I also have Lane Assist.
I NEVER use Lane Assist for a few reasons namely the feedback thru the steering wheel it's like you're always fighting it, the car chooses where it wants to be in the lane and often it's too close to centerline like a 2 lane hwy (I prefer to drive over to the right in the lane, very often Lane Assist shuts down because it can't "see" the lines or there a gap in the road lines, Lane assist IMO is kind of unsafe (you cannot rely on it) so I never use it luckily unlike Tesla Autopilot I can shut off Lane Assist and still have Adaptive Cruise Control (which I Love) they're actually independent from each other  That's why I'd NEVER get a Tesla. Autopilot has merged 2 different functions and can not be separated not yet anyway maybe a software update could separate?
You didn't mention "PHANTOM BRAKING" (look it up) it's a major issue with Model 3 and Model Y and can be very dangerous the car can suddenly brake form any speed and come to a stop imagine that on a freeway...Phantom Braking happens when Autopilot is engaged! I can't help but wonder why Tesla integrated cruise control with autopilot...BIG mistake IMO. They lost me as a potential customer at least until they separate cruise control from lane assist so they're independent from each other.

text:
I've owned both (Model 3 LR & Seal Excellence) & my short advice to anybody that's considering buying either:

Seats - M3 is comfier for longer even though initially the Seal feels better (not as much under thigh support is the problem I think, the back seats are much better in the Seal than the M3 though)
Performance - M3 accelerator pedal is more snappy / responsive, the Seal's pedal feels slightly muted even in Sport but overall the Seal pushes you back in the seat harder when you give it a bootful
Chassis - M3 is more nimble / tight / agile, the Seal is more comfy & better damped but will wallow more (slightly) into corners as the suspension loads up, you can also feel the extra 400KGs of the Seal
Brakes / Regen braking - M3 brake pedal feels more wooden but you hardly use it due to regen braking, the Seal's pedal has more travel & feels more spongy but does have more feel, it can be grabby at very slow speeds though. You use the brake pedal more on the Seal as the regen braking is less forceful
Controls - M3 gear select & indicators take some getting used to but you do, the touch screen is more responsive & has better resolution, the Seal has had some software updates since this video was done & controls are easy to get to with a bottom, customisable menu on the main screen. I prefer the Seal as it feels more like a "traditional" car, especially with the HUD & digital driver display.
Range / charging - I would regularly trust the M3 to get me home even at 5% projected battery from a long drive, you can trust the projected mileage even at 80mph on the motorway, the Seal has less range than claimed by a long distance & I dont trust the range projected as much as the Tesla. Charging outside of the Tesla Supercharger network is like the Wild West & more expensive. The last update to the Seal now provides suggested charge points on the route but is isn't as good as the Tesla option

Final thought - drive them both, see what you prefer but if range & cost per mile is the most important consideration for you, buy the Tesla. For comparison, I drive my M3 exactly the same as I drove any other ICE car before & it returned 4.3miles/kW over the 9k miles I owned it, the Seal is giving me 3.1 miles/kW in the 3k miles I've had it so far.

text: I drove a brand new Rolls Royce Ghost.  All the climate controls were knobs, sliders, buttons, etc.  I'll be buying 1 owner used pre-screen vehicles until manufactures re-release controls that you can operate by memory without taking your eyes off the road.  Also, screen menus are slow and cumbersome.  Imagine how frustrated people are around you when you are focused on your menus (parking for example).  Amazing how all those years we successfully parked our cars without screens/cameras.  It was a skill driver's needed to learn.  Range loss and charge time continue to be the primary factors for widespread EV adoption.   We drove some Teslas 460 miles in the Colorado Mountains, with a mix of mountain passes, canyons, state highway cruising, and interstate at 75+.  We had to charge 3 times for about 45 minutes each charge.  And the charging stations had no services (bathroom, food, etc.).  Just parking lots and chargers.  In the heat of summer the range loss is around 50%.  The use case for EV's is still limited.

I tested Tesla Model 3 (before facelift) and BYD Seal, and with the 3YO and wife on the backseat.  The 3YO puked in the Tesla when driving around curvy roads, and falls asleep in the BYD seal.  The update notice that came before you did your test said they had added a drift mode, and that's probably what you have seen.  It's only available in sports mode, and you can improve it by turning off ESC mode (it's not completely off, it will kick in at above 80km/h if the drifting gets out of control).  I use Eco and normal mode, and don't use sports mode, and haven't seen anything like that, i.e. on normal driving conditions.  Well, I also replaced the EcoContact 6 tires with Michelin CrossClimate 2, and they do have better grip in cold wet conditions.
Overall, both braking pedals (not much force required) and steering wheel feel Citroën-like (DIRAVI style with no feedback but speed-dependent force), and might take some time to get used to.  I had a Citroën before, so I felt at home.  While the brakes needed to be pushed gently, the accelerator needs to be pushed deliberately to get full power.  Generally, the BYD the way more comfortable car, compared to the Model 3 before facelift.  Also, Elon Musk makes it really, really difficult to buy a product. text:
BYD Seal Excellence owner here, my views are this:

- It’s very fast off the line, not so much at higher speeds, cuts off at 120mph
- Looks amazing inside and out 
- Very comfortable to drive 
- Lots of gadgets and settings that take getting used to; once you’ve got it set up and understand it all it’s fine, only issue is traffic warning needs turning off each time 
- Stereo system is great
- Voice control for most features
- Apple Car Play is great, getting a 3rd party bridge Carlinkit to make full screen mirror and other app use to work eg Netflix / YouTube 
- The front parking sensors are useless, kick in at 50cm (but if you look it’s much less than 50cm imo)
- Rear parking sensors too quiet 
- Range is nowhere near what they say. I drove in eco, standard range (not dynamic), turned AC off, turned screen off, brake regen on high and a 20 mile journey knocked 40 miles off my battery; perhaps in warmer weather it’ll be less noticeable 

It’s a great car all in all though, real head turner, you won’t see many about and it’ll leave a dual motor Tesla M for dust at take off from traffic lights, unless it’s the performance model.

text:
The new interface in the Model 3 is ghastly.  I hate the indicators as the controls don't fit my driving style.  But, the previous generate Model 3 (while a bit bumpier in the back seats and a tiny bit louder) is immense fun.  I ordinarily dislike single track rural roads with lumps of horse excrement in the middle, with the phrase "risk of grounding" floating continually in my mind, but the Tesla makes driving even those horrible roads fun and easy.  HOWEVER, the Model 3 needs an update to its camera lenses: they need either a rotating ball, and/or a cleaning solution.  They also need high definition night cameras because if you get caught in a country lane, as I have, and need to reverse, then all you can rely on are your mirrors (in an unlit lane with stone walls either side), or your cameras which only show you where your going when the brake lights come on as you inevitably panic about scratching your lovely new car, while simultaneously annoying the local who has driven the stretch of road a million times, in a tractor, and could easily let a coach get through.  This, as a result, can make a reasonably good driver *appear* thick.  Those are my main criticisms.

Oh, and don't take a Tesla Model 3 to a muddy field without "Slip Mode" activated.  I instantly buried 30% of the wheels as a result.  It made me *appear* thick ;)

text:
You Have Problems, Not Issues
Somewhere, at some point over the recent past, someone decided that it was no longer acceptable for a person to say what he or she means; it was no longer acceptable to speak in precise, direct words. And what’s worse, someone, somewhere decided that we should all be offended when someone calls a problem a problem. Everything has to be translated into some sort of euphemism. I don’t really know why it started, but can we please stop referring to every problem as an issue?

An employee no longer has a problem keeping up with production; he has an issue. A child no longer has a problem behaving in class; she has an issue. A married couple in therapy no longer has problems in their marriage; they have issues.

Even bad weather now causes performance issues on the football field and traffic issues on the road; and a basketball player with a sprained ankle has an ankle issue. I’m not sure what’s so offensive about discussing traffic problems, health problems, or a sloppy football game. Is it just me?

The problem—that is, what’s wrong—with substituting issue for problem is that those two words are not synonymous—and no amount of being politically correct, disingenuous, or even condescending—yes, it can be condescending—will make it so.

An issue is a topic, such as The candidates will discuss the issues at the debate. That means that the candidates will discuss the different topics, or subject areas, involved in running our country.

A problem is something negative. A problem is something that needs to be solved. A problem is something that we try to overcome. A problem is something that we don’t want. There, I’ve said it. And it feels great.

An issue is not a problem, but I’ll tell you what is a problem: the grammatically incorrect trend of telling someone that he has an issue when what you really mean is that he has a problem. Call it what it is, and it’ll be easier to solve.

text:
Tesla has taken cost cutting too far, and it has now made the car frustrating to drive, sadly. The turn signal buttons on the steering wheel are extremely annoying to use in tight roundabouts, because it forces you to constantly look down at the wheel in a critical situation when your eyes really should be on the road. It's a safety concern!

They are also not always responsive, and will require you to try again. It is also far to easy to press the wrong button. You will know if you pressed a stalk up or down, but you have no way of knowing if you pressed the correct button, unless you take your eyes off the road again and look down when pressing, or at the screen to confirm.

The wiper button is also moved to the wheel, which I don't like. Wouldn't have been a problem if the auto wipers were the best in the business, but they're not. In fact they're the worst, so you're going to be using that manual wiper button a lot.. 
The AP button is also unresponsive at times. It doesn't always register double taps, even though I can clearly hear it clicks twice. And the high beams also automatically comes on when engaging the AP, blinding other cars, so you constantly have to turn them off. 

I can live with the gear selector on the screen, but honestly, this too is a downgrade. Particularly in tight parking garages for example, when you need to do a lot of back and forward motion. Before you could change direction while looking around at the same time. Now you have to look at the screen to swipe instead, so it's more tedious and slower than before, and it makes you less aware of your surroundings. 
All this just makes the car really annoying to drive, particularly when there are tight roundabouts everywhere, which tend to be the case here in the EU. 

They also removed the ultrasonic parking sensors, and the new camera-based system is so inaccurate that it's basically useless now. Fog lights are also removed, and I also miss a dedicated instrument cluster or a HUD. Apparently they're now also going to downgrade the stereo to just 7 speakers. What's next? Virtual steering wheel on the screen? That would surely make the car even cheaper!

It's just sad that they've opted to remove so many useful functions to cut costs, because the rest of the car is actually great, but due to these stupid decisions it becomes frustrating to drive, and I don't like spending good money on a car that constantly annoys me...

text:
I guess the lack of  a central speedo or HUD explains why Teslas are driven at either 50mph in the middle lane of the motorway or 70 mph on residential roads. The drivers have no idea what speed they are travelling.

As for the bright white seats, I suppose the majority of Teslas are driven by company reps who don't have kids. And the two grand for a colour explains why so many are white, company fleet managers won't pay for that.

The lack of physical controls is a massive red flag for me. No car should take weeks or months to learn to drive. A few days for the idiosyncrasies of the lesser used controls maybe. But indicators, gears/drive selectors etc should be second nature the instant you get  behind the wheel. I don't want fart apps. I don't want Mario kart rip off games. 

I want a safe car that myself and other members of my family can just drive without having to refer to the owners manual just to put it in reverse.

Just about every review that mentions EV in general or Tesla specifically will mention the wonders of the supercharger network. Well, for me, it's a benefit that's of little use. I don't work hundreds of miles from home. I don't have to travel for work. In the 18 months we've owned an EV, I've plugged it into a public charger once, just to see how it worked. It worked fine. I charge at home, far cheaper than any public network, so you can keep your wonder network, it's no use to me.

We have two cars. One a small city EV, the other a diesel 4x4. Neither of these EVs are suitable replacements for ours. Tesla do not make a car than can replace either. They don't do small city cars and their attempts at an SUV is the laughable Model X. Stupid rear doors that mean you can't put cycles on the roof, stupidly expensive and virtually every Model X on the UK Tesla website, when selecting the New car option, is an ex-Demo car. I've never seen any other manufacturer class ex-Demo cars with thousands of miles on the clock as New.  Oh, and the final feature of the Model X in the UK? "Only available as left-hand drive".

Auto-pilot that isn't New cars that aren't new. Steering wheel on the wrong side. Why do people like Tesla?

text:
Tesla ruined the Model 3 with the new steering wheel. I hate the new wheel designs and I wouldn’t ever buy one that was missing surround cameras, parking sensors, adaptive dampers, HUD, or cross traffic detection. Tesla is also falling behind on the charging speeds against cars like the Ioniq 6. As a former Model 3P owner there’s just not enough new to make me excited about the Highland 3. My 2019 3P had more hardware than the brand new one and I didn’t have to rely on the unreliable cameras to judge how close I was to objects. Tesla vision is horrendously unreliable. My experience in multiple recent Ys and 3s has confirmed Tesla Vision has no idea how close objects are in reality. It often sees phantom things or doesn’t see things at all. Elon needs to stop taking features out.  The vast majority of Model 3 owners do not care about having a small display for passengers in the rear. A basic climate control panel with buttons for heated seats would’ve been just fine and cheaper. Instead, as I mentioned, I’m sure the average consumer would much rather have more cameras, radar front and rear for cross traffic detection, a HUD, driver display, or massaging seats instead. For this, the BYD is a better buy, but I would go for an Ioniq 6, Ioniq 5N, EV6 GT or i4 before I bought either of these.

Also, Mat, the 10-80% charge in a Model 3 is about 28 minutes, not 14. The car doesn’t maintain 250kW for more than a few minutes. By 50% it’s dropped down to around 125kW. By 80% you’re below 80kW. The fastest charging cars from 10-80% are the Hyundai/Kia/Genesis e-GMP cars that offer an 18 minute charge time.

text:
I’m the fleet manager for our company group. We have 50 vehicles. We are located in the alps and we need vehicles that perform well in steep and winding roads. We have decided to slowly pass to electric due to low maintenance, low fuel cost, and also because in the mountain roads the electric cars usually perform really well. They have a nice kick, that is useful to pass slow vehicles, and thanks to regen downhill the advantage on fuel costs becomes even greater than on the flat  compared to ICE, because all the potential energy of an ICE vehicle downhill gets dissipated in heat at the breaks or using the low gears to slow down. while in an EV is put back in the battery.
Or at least this is what Teslas do. We already have one in the fleet. So that is a fact for me.
Due to image issues I wasn’t planning to buy more teslas, and pass to BYD. So I tested 2 of them. Unfortunately the regen is too weak even at the strongest level. I was forced to use the breaks all the way down. And that is bad. Not only because I’m not recovering all the potential energy, but mostly because I risk of overheating the breaks. And that is really bad. So until they don’t come with a more powerful regen setup BYD is a no for us. I really don’t get why BYD doesn’t improve on that part. For the rest are beautiful cars. The interior are far better than teslas and and the cars seems overall more solid and there is a wider choice, so I could have accommodated all the different needs with just one brand, that means just one shop for the maintenance.

The windscreen wipers was never an issue. Actually having the button on the wheel makes it much more intuitive to wash the windscreen when its not raining and dirt gets kicked up from the motorway. 

The steering rake is literally something you do once. And while you should absolutely not be adjusting it whole driving, its absolutely possible and far safer than trying to pull a steering wheel around while you're driving. 

Honestly, I'd recommend anyone with a family or anyone over 6ft this car. Its the best car I've ever owned and I've been an Audi driver for the last 17 years.

text:
I've tested both these cars and I've got to say that many things were wrong in this video. First thing is that the BYD Sealion or any BYD, has no Youtube, Netflix or anything similar integrated into the infotainment system, especially when the screen looks so bad (on all models). You can however use Apple Carplay or Android Auto to mirror it, but the quality is just bad and it will be using your phone's data unlike the Teslas having their own data. On the Tesla, many people still use Netflix, Youtube and the rest while charging, it's not really a gimmick but a comfort. These cars having 14 speakers makes you enjoy films like you're in a cinema, especially late at night when it's darker.

The doors on the Tesla are quite straightforward and I would even say very nice to use. They blend in well with the car's shape and the interior door button is very satisfying to use, seems luxurious but, many new passengers still try to pull on the emergency lever thinking it's the main door lever.
The autonomy, speed, interior space, infotainment, charging prices, aftersales support, quality and how easy it is to drive, all goes to Tesla without a doubt. The things that they messed up like the stalks and the lack of buttons can be fixed with simple aftermarket mods that actually work amazingly well and are very responsive.
Also, driving the Sealion is horrible. It wobbles horribly on corners and it even bounces sometimes when accelerating from 0mph and is unstable. Reminds me much of the Mustang GT Performance, which I also disliked a lot, especially when I actually love Fords.

This video feels very biased against Tesla and could either be a silent sponsorship or politics.

My verdict as an actual car tester: Teslas are great cars, if not, the best on the current market.

text: As an electrical engineer, I laugh every time I hear someone claim a Chinese product is equal to or better than a something made in the US or Germany or France or Japan. If you go through the brands that are used far and wide across industries for simple electrical and electronic needs, you come up with names like Omron, Telemecanique, Siemens, Schneider, GE, Honeywell and so on. A step down would be Hyundai, LS and Delta. If you've ever worked with electrical equipment, servo/step motors or even simple traditional squirrel-cage motors, you'd know the difference between a pure Chinese product and one that comes from a reputable company, even one that has its production line in China. Everything from the ball bearings to the dimensions of the copper wire and in most cases even the copper in the wire itself vastly differ in quality. The end result is that when the damn thing is new, you can see a small difference between the two that can't justifying paying so much more for a reputable brand. But once a year or two passes, you start noticing just how subpar Chinese products really are.

text:
Some useful tesla-related advice and recommendations from experience:

1. Mirrors - you can click the steering wheel roller to toggle between left/right mirror.
2. You can add a few quick selection buttons at the bottom of the screen (I like having the seats, steering wheel heating, windshield defog).
3. You can quickly change AC temperature by just swiping left/right with your finger and it you dont have to take your eyes off the road (I even put a "macro" on the left steering wheel scroller which when held for 1s let's me adjust temp by scrolling without taking my hands off the wheel).
4. Android Auto/apple car play - the tesla maps are just the google api so it's exactly the same, plus if you like searching for a favourite saved place on your maps app through your phone you can just click "share" on google maps and select the tesla app, it will send it to your car's screen.
5. Spotify and youtube music come as part of the tesla OS, I don't have the premium versions so I just used a cracked youtube music on my phone and play it through bluetooth, it starts playing as soon as I enter the car so it there's no let-downs from my use case.
6. Suspension - it's one of the most comfortable suspensions I've ever felt (I've only ever had renaults, VWs, older BMWs so it's as close to luxury as my poor ass has ever been).

Just adding my perspective here, having sat in both latest versions, and having driven both the earlier versions.

Without a doubt, Tesla is nicer to drive, feels cleaner (but obviously not car-like due to weight/shape, so we aren't talking much on dynamics/feel here.)

In my country, it has the better charging network, faster to charge, can drive longer etc.

But, I get Matt's review. Tesla is, in almost every measurable way, better than BYD.

But BYD actually feels like a car, not a laptop with wheels. The interior feels soooo much better in real life, the door sounds, materials you touch etc. "feels" a lot more premium to actually touch.

I don't know if there's some bias in the video above because he was quite upfront on how Tesla won everything measurable. But, between the two cars, having tested them, my money goes to BYD.

(Actually, It did. Expecting delivery in late May/Early June. Although I got the PHEV that I can put petrol as well together with some electric range)

text:
I wouldn't go so easily with the BYD. 
I mean, I love the looks, interior and ergonomics of the BYD rather than the Tesla.
But I have watched other tests, some of them driven by actual engineers and test drivers and the BYD, even the AWD, is much focused on comfort rather than road handling.
Also, the software in the Tesla is years ahead of the BYD. Some people say that this can be fixed, however the BYD is using regular Android, which I think will limit its capability to be updated in the future (note, this is not Android Automotive, whoever who has owned an Honda will know what and Android system works).
Nevertheless, ADAS are much worse than a Tesla or any other major brand. Have you tried to disable the speed alarm? In the Tesla is just one touch, in the BYD you have to dive into 3 menus. And you have to do this every time you start the car.
The battery is bigger but the car is less efficient and the range is aligned with a Model 3 SR (and much lower than a LR).
And I have questions about how the APP works. This is something crucial in EVs to control charge and pre-climate and the Tesla APP works smoothly.
On the other hand, the BYD has a radar, camera, a proper rain sensor and parking sensors. Not so cool as the Tesla Vision but should work better is everything is calibrated properly.

I mean, I love and hate both cars. Both have good arguments to buy and to discard them. Just disagreeing in a so categoric answer.
Maybe if Tesla creates a sub-brand with "normal" designs and ergonomics...

text:
I first watched this video with increasing amazement and later, to make sure I had seen and heard all of this correctly, again. And indeed, it showed two ladies, one of whom quite credibly tried to maintain a certain distance from the subject and the other, to the point of being hilarious, showed her disgust uninhibitedly.

The lack of traditional functionality turned out to be the biggest and ultimately insurmountable breaking point, while this should all mainly be about traditional versus more future-oriented car designs and what car manufacturers choose or not and how they sometimes even fall back on concepts that have been around for much longer. And which by the way will never or can never be completely perfect in all respects because: humans at work.

It is more honest to make an inventory of the different properties and compare them with each other. That comes across as more sincere in terms of content than a story full of vitriol, full of pretended benevolence, excellently written, that's for sure, but here and there ostentatiously over-acted. Ultimately it's just a matter of personal preference, nothing more. Everything else is theater.

text:
I have a Model Y but the seats in the Seal do look more comfortable but my seats are way more comfortable than my gas car so I love them. 

I'm fine with the minimalist interior of Tesla. It's one reason I bought it. I've had plenty of cars like the BYD with dust collecting buttons I rarely use. And I'm so over companies using cheap shinny plastic buttons. 

Here's what matters to me in this test. BYD is more expensive, heavier, less efficient, not so good regenerative braking, less cargo space and the cockpit area seemed a little more cramped than the Tesla. And comparing these two, the Seal isn't all wheel drive and it's something you have to upgrade to making it even more expensive compared to this Tesla model.

The BYD Seal is a decent looking car but sort of a mixture between a Hyundai Elantra and an Xpeng. The Model 3, to me, has sleeker body lines. The BYD tail lights are nice.

I'd also say for us here in the US, one of the biggest differences between the two is the BYD Seal doesn't have any Autopilot features. On long road trips that's a deal breaker for me. May not be an issue across the pond where you may be restricted from having/using it.

Overall if you want something other than the Tesla the Seal is nice but for bang for the buck the Tesla Model 3 is the better choice...and I say all of this as a Tesla and BYD investor.

Interesting take, I disagree with the reviewers opinion on the road feel and handling of the 2 cars - the new Tesla is superior to the BYD, not that the BYD is bad it's pretty good as well, I just can't understand how anyone who has driven both cars can possibly say the BYD has superior road manners to the Tesla.

I think they are similarly quiet, the Tesla definitely has more storage room, and the Technology implementation is vastly superior to the BYD despite the BYD having a few more features like 360 view etc. We don't have any longitudinal evidence on durability yet so hard to tell but as cars they are pretty close but the Tech and cabin for me swing it in favour of the Tesla - the BYD interior is more familiar to people coming from ICE cars so some may find it less confronting but I personally like the fact that the Tesla has no buttons and dials outside of the screen and steering wheel. 

The lack of stalks on the Tesla was a bad idea this brings the BYD back into play - overall as cars I think they are pretty close - (personal styling preferences aside I think the new Tesla is massively better looking than the BYD which I think already looks really dated)

The thing that swings the equation big time back in Tesal's favour is tech & charging - with the latest update the Tesla will gather all of the data for all other Tesla's following similar routes to your journey and using AI will detrmine the best charger & charging strategy to get you to your destination in the shortest possible time by aggregating all of the information it has on who is likely to reach chargers at what time and for how long they will spend there. BYD are nowhere near this level of sophistication - but in Australia they are also $3k cheaper like for like and they also have a $10k cheaper base model - tough choice but I would go with the Tesla (and even more so if it had stalks)

text: Perhaps I'm odd but, whenever I see negative reviews of the M3's "instrument" placement, I begin to wonder if I'm the only human who has the ability to move their eyes from side to side! When facing forward, looking straight ahead at the road, the Tesla's speedometer display is well within my line of sight: If I want to look at it directly, I need only shift my eyes 30° in that direction - exactly the same amount I shift them in the opposite direction to see the side-view mirror on the driver's door. (And, yes, I did indeed sit there with a protractor on my nose.) Why YouTube commentators all demonstrate the inconvenience of having to move their entire head to see the display is beyond me. To view a "conventional" speedometer (peering through the steering wheel), a driver needs to drop their eyes some 60° - surely THAT action is more "dangerous". Funny thing, though, is that I can't recall ANYONE complaining when the Prius and the Mini had their gauges in the center of the dash...

text:
Nice to have a review on the RWD Seal, as most reviews are on the AWD version, but finally a few are coming through on the RWD version.
Interesting how in the UK the Seal costs more than the Tesla. Here in Australia the Mid spec Seal with the larger battery (as in this review) is ~AUD 4k cheaper than the entry level M3 Highland.
Prices vary as well. The on road (driveaway) cost of the two BYD Seal versions here in AUS that are the same as in the UK (although we have a cheaper entry level Seal down here as well) are Seal Premium 230kw motor with larger battery at ~AUD63k (~33.5 GBP) and the Performance 390kw motor AWD (Excellence) ~AUD73k (~39k GBP) The entry level Seal with a 150kw motor (same as in the Atto 3) and 18 inch wheels is ~53k driveaway.

I totally agree with the comment on lack of one pedal driving. Perhaps it could be added in a software update (or perhaps not that simple?) I drove an MG4, where you could select one pedal mode in the menu. But it was too severe. Needs a slider control for personal preference within certain parameters. Tesla have it pretty much right. I also recently drove the M3 update and was quite impressed and am waiting to drive the Seal before ordering.

LOL, yes, the M3 does feel a bit like driving a robot. Just a bit too minimalist for me, but still nice.

text:
作为一个中国的海豹车主我表达一下我的看法（我就懒得写英语了，反正你们可以用谷歌翻译），特斯拉在上海的销量非常的好，所以我可以很容易的从我的朋友那试驾他们的model3和model Y ，通过试驾我自己体会了记得让我很不舒服的地方，1. 特斯拉没有专门的仪表盘，这让我不得不在行驶过程中不停的看中央屏幕来获取速度信息避免超速。 2. 单踏板模式，我非常不理解单踏板给你们（欧洲人/美州人）带来的所谓便利性，在我看来这会让一个习惯了传统汽车驾驶的司机在使用特斯拉时变成一个马路杀手（中国的汽车驾驶培训告诉我们的驾驶方式是非常根深蒂固的）。3. 特斯拉的内饰， （尽管我还没有尝试过新的model3听说他升级了不错的内饰）特斯拉对于内饰的偷工减料简直是在犯罪 他们用20多万RMB的价格卖出的汽车  内饰甚至不如一台10万RMB的大众汽车。
回到我选择比亚迪的理由 1. 作为一个中国汽车品牌，他在中国的售价确实比较的划算。 2.  比亚迪的充电协议使它支持中国市场上可以看到的所有充电桩（包括特斯拉的特高压800V超级充电桩，顺便说一句中国的公共充电桩数量超过全世界的总和）3. 海豹的驾驶感受更像一台汽油动力的轿车。4. 很多评论中提到的能量回收的可调节范围 海豹有高动能回收和普通回收两个档位，你们可以从屏幕左下角的汽车小标识点击进入后设置。 5.  虽然比亚迪的智能化水平在中国电动车厂家里算是一个悲剧但是他的语音识别能力还是不错的，很多时候你们可以直接通过语音发布指令。

text:
@newbris I test drove the Model 3 RWD and LR for 45mins each. There’s absolutely no doubts there’s a huge upgrade over the previous Model 3 and does everything better.

The main talking point is obviously the stalk removal. Gave them a good workout in varying scenarios and while they weren’t really an issue and it took minimal time to get use to them there were times where they were simply an inconvenience and these situations can’t be avoided based simply on hand/wheel positioning.

Ride comfort and cabin noise improvements are certainly noticeable on smooth roads but still got some noise at highway speeds.

The main issue but not really an issue given it’s in beta was the auto-gear selector. Only got to try it a few times but on a couple of occasions it made the wrong selection and if you were none-the-wiser it could be a rather ominous outcome. I have seen previous videos where Tesla Vision has grossly misjudged objects and measurements so hopefully there’s improvements there.

The other things I’m not a big fan of: gear selection on the centre screen, exterior looks, everything on the centre screen and completely minimalist look and feel.

Overall I was impressed with the upgraded Model 3 but ultimately, I still prefer the look of both the interior and exterior of the Seal and for the money, I still can’t go past it. The (Tesla) RWD in my preferred config would be $70K ($64K after the rebate) and the LR would be $80K while the Seal Performance is $72K.

Teslas are too minimalistic... to an extent, that you start missing things that are more practical: mainly stalks and physical buttons. text: 53k miles on a M3, extended test drive on the BYD Seal. The BYD is definitely a more comfortable car to travel in with great quality materials and ride comfort and sound insulation. I also think the BYD looks a bit better. The cabin and the seats are top quality and the exterior is also really nice, looks even better in person. But the M3 (even the old one) is just a bit more fun to drive. Its direct and darty (which I like) charges WAY faster, has the network and also a very large service network. The BYD is in its infancy, driving 100 miles to a service centre at the moment isnt ideal....UI wise the Teslas are also miles ahead. Menus make sense and are intuitive and grouped properly ie Climate/Display/Controls etc. The BYD has a bit of everything everywhere. Menus, pull downs, side swipes. That being said the Seals central screen is something special its so large and so crisp when navigating its a joy. Its also worth noting according BYD any Seals shipped before March come with the indicator on the right stalk and wipers on the left. My test car had this and was a nightmare to adjust to. Apparently the norm in other right drive markets. It also has the most aggressive lane departure system Ive ever seen (Even more aggressive than the MG4). Even an few inches left or right of centre it was dragging you all over the place. Can be turned off no doubt but needs adjusting. Id deffo still recommend it but I think it still needs some maturity and bug ironing to make it a sure thing. Most of that can be done through software so should be easy. Credit to them though honestly it rides as well a C Class/3 Series maybe even a smidgeon better. There arent many EVs that can do that. The new Tesla indicator is a no go for me too 🤣 the New M3 ups its quality considerably but not enough to tempt me for one either... so I'll be hanging on to my old M3 for now. If anyone has one, that would be my advice, especially if like me you still have ultrasonic sensors 🤣 (If you know you know....)

text:
You can still play music from a USB on a newer Model 3, but it requires some trickery. If you're comfortable with computers, you could replace the sentry USB stick in the glovebox with a larger device, ideally a "real" SSD (which use higher quality flash memory that's far more durable than any USB stick). Connect it to a computer and format it with two partitions, one for sentry and another for music.

Or you can connect a hub in the glovebox USB port, use one port for the sentry USB stick and another for your music. Tesla explicitly advises against this, however.

Finally there are aftermarket USB port modules for the centre console which give you more ports including one which supports data connections.

text:
When Tesla announced the new Model 3 with switches for indicators as a driver trainer I started to think about the implications for driving safely. You can be sure if Tesla is doing this other manufacturers will follow. It keeps production costs down and some legacy manufacturers need to find savings if they stand any chance of avoiding bankruptcy in the transition to EVs. 

So I started to watch my trainees with indicator buttons in mind. After a couple of Nissan Leafs I now own a Model 3. Surprisingly I noticed there’s a lot of times when trainees have to let go of the steering wheel with their left hand and move it back to the stalk when their hand would be next to the buttons if they kept hold of the wheel. I’ll qualify this with the fact that a Model 3 only does one turn to lock and is very responsive. Rarely was anyone more than a quarter turn from straight when they needed to indicate. The right turn on a roundabout and signalling left to leave is the example that could cause problems because I noticed the steering wheel was generally upside down at this point.

So I thought about this right turn on a roundabout and the upside down steering wheel. Then I noticed myself subconsciously turning the radio volume up on the steering wheel control whatever way it’s pointing. Upside down, sideways, it doesn’t matter where the steering is pointing I’ve developed the skill of using that control. My conclusion is button indicators are just a different skill. A new learner who only ever saw that system would probably find stalks weird. I equate it to training I’ve done with experienced licence holders of many years first encountering an automatic. They are perplexed initially but like it when they get used to it. 

The Tesla Model 3 does divide opinion. Personally, I love it. I find the minimalist interior calming and a very nice place to spend the day. The lack of clutter in the car focuses trainees minds. When it’s not doing it’s day job I really like the firm ride and direct steering. I also think it’s a good looking car. The Supercharger network is a number 1 reason to get a Tesla, drive anywhere with no concern about charging. 

However, people have different tastes and we need a cars to cater for different tastes. Legacy manufacturers can’t get near Tesla despite trying hard. The worlds top selling car this year will be the Model Y and Tesla will sell almost as many cars as BMW or Mercedes, that’s cars regardless of powertrains not just EVs. We need a new competitive car market to emerge. BYD look like they will be commercial challengers to Tesla. The Seal is a good competitor, similar but different appealing to different customers. Those that feel reassured by a car closer to the ICE they’re giving up on will feel more comfortable with the Seal.  BYD will also be filling the low end sector with the Seagull and Dolphin where Tesla have no models as yet. The thing about this is that the new world car market will be dominated by the Chinese and Tesla. Interesting times.

text:
@patmanrick I will bite as a Seal owner who had an order on an Model 3 HL as well before test driving both back to back and deciding on the Seal.

- The more storage was nice, for sure. At least as far as the boot goes, as a family it would definitely be easier for us with a M3 but if I truly cared that much I also wouldn't be buying a sedan but an SUV. The interior space storage wise is a lot more usable on the Seal on the other hand, with more nooks and crannies to store stuff. 

- In terms of charging faster, the difference in peak charge rate is only 20kw which is much of muchness. Yes the M3 charges faster but that has more to do with the size of the batteries, with the Seal Premium having a 20kw bigger battery. In reality this means that it takes about 13 minutes extra to get the same 10-80 charge. Yes that is a decent difference, and I do very much wish the charging was faster - BUT - the only time I use DC chargers is when taking longer journeys and with the Seal that means I need to stop roughly every 3 or so hours for a charge, which is what we do anyway as a family with young kids who need to run around for half an hour to not scream the roof off. So either way, whether we had M3 or Seal our journey routine and length would be pretty much the same. 

- The M3 does have better software without a doubt, no argument from me. But also, I'm buying a car not a phone, the software is only one part of the puzzle and part of the reason the rest of my family said no after the test drive was that the M3 felt too much like a mix between an iPhone and a fridge. It's an appliance made by a tech company, not a car made by an auto-maker. That's not an objectively bad thing, and I personally don't mind it as much being in tech myself - but the rest of my family hated it. And besides, the software in the BYD isn't that bad, hell it's better than most traditional auto-makers and that's more than enough for me. And because it's based on Android I've been able to ADB in and do some interesting stuff. The ADAS in the Tesla is mostly better, but I honestly don't think Tesla Vision is as amazing as a lot of other people do, and it has it's own issues. Most of the Seal's issues come down to calibration, as honestly they've just been lazy on that front and haven't done the hard yards of properly calibrating and programming the ADAS for the different countries environments. In China it works fine, not as good as Tesla still and not as good as some of the other rivals but it's fine which is the only bar I really care about as someone that daily drives another car with 'fine' ADAS systems and doesn't have an issue. 

- The ventilation and heating isn't an issue in Australia, both the long range Premium model (about $3k less than the base M3 here) and the entry level Dynamic model (about $13k less) here come with seat heating and ventilation as standard. 

- As for price see above. I completely understand the calculations being different when pricing is different though, and I would have had a much harder time deciding if I was in the UK or EU. With Australian pricing though it was a no brainer. 

- Rear screen doesn't bother me personally, and I think it looks kind of ugly and tacked on, but it is a cool feature. Netflix and other apps are eventually meant to be coming to the BYD, you can already sideload a bunch of stuff, and there's a browser that you can watch various stuff on built in (I use it mostly for YouTube when charging, but generally I find it easier to just use my phone regardless of Tesla or BYD, ditto for games), Dog mode/camp mode etc are super cool and are a big boon to the Tesla and something I hope comes to the BYD one day, same with Sentry which is an amazing Tesla feature that I genuinely love. No doubt that Tesla offers a lot of cool little functions that are nice to haves. 

- I don't mind one pedal driving, but both my partner and Mum (who will be driving it a lot as we're a multi-generational household) can't stand it on the few cars they've driven with it. Personally I would rather BYD add it and have it able to be turned down, than to just not have it, but it's not a feature I would pay extra for either. I do want to note also that the Seal has just as good regenerative braking as the Model 3, it's just blended into the brake pedal rather than the one pedal system, so you're not losing the actual benefits of regenerative braking, you're just losing using it without using the brake pedal. This was done on purpose to make it feel like a traditional car rather than... well a Tesla - I don't think that's a good or bad thing, it's just a different design choice. 

- Tesla is amazing at efficiency, that absolutely can't be argued. The Seal is pretty good, and is better than most other EV's on that front, but Tesla's are still the kings of efficiency and the amount of range they can pull out of relatively modest batteries is pretty amazing. 

- The difference between the safety scores is hard to compare, Tesla hasn't been tested to NCAP/ANCAP 2023, only 2019 which isn't as strict. The Seal has been, and achieved only a modestly lower rating than what the Model 3 achieved to the less strict 2019 testing. It scored a little worse on adult occupant, the same on child, better on pedestrian, and decently worse on driving assistance - but take that with some salt as that's the area of the testing that has become a lot more strict since 2019. I would say they're pretty equivalent rather than the M3 being outright much better. I would still probably say the Model 3 is slightly safer purely on ADAS, but we'll see how much once it get's retested.

text: @EcoHouseThailand   Yes, but Harry is right here. The reason why needed for me a lot of googeling: The top Voltage of a Lfp Battery is a lot lower than on a Nmc Battery, but the Low end operating Voltage is about the same, so the Range of Voltage between Full and Empty is lower, but the Voltage is with what the Battery Management System is figuring out how much Charge is left and because of the lower range of Voltage it is a lot harder for the Bms with a Lfp Battery to figure out the actuall Charge than with the more often used Nmc Battery. With charging it to 100% the Bms learns best the actual charge and the more often in a row you don't charge to 100% the more little failures are coming in the calculation, which is a lot worse in Lfp Batteries. So because Lfp Batteries lasts 3 times longer than Nmc Batteries, there is no need in protecting the Battery, because the Lfp Battery will easily outlive every car they're in, as Nmc Batterys already nearly do that. So yes, also a Lfp Battery would last longer if you don't charge it to 100%, but it doesn't really matter and you could end up stranded because the Bms calculated the SoC wrong.
